item.title: OpenAI pulls out of Caltech math hackathon after mathematicians issue open letter criticizing AI math 'slop'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.08
The latest math problem OpenAI is trying to solve is a bunch of angry mathematicians. A researcher at OpenAI said on Thursday that the ChatGPT maker is no longer sponsoring Caltech's "math hackathon," an event where participants use large language models to solve research problems. OpenAI's exit follows an open letter released on Wednesday from current and former Caltech mathematicians, who said the event, which is sponsored by AI companies, "is likely to have destructive impacts for the mathematical community." "We recognize that the rapid progress of AI in mathematics is disruptive," Dan Roberts, OpenAI's research lead, said on X. "We're looking to engage with the math community more on the best way to integrate this technology and communicate its impacts." At issue, according to the mathematicians, is the manner in which AI companies claim to solve outstanding theoretical problems using their models and then leave practical applications and proofs to actual researchers. They call this "slop mathematics." "After the latest result is dropped, research mathematicians are compelled to step in to properly verify, disseminate, and sometimes discredit entirely the claimed results," the academics said. "This labor goes uncompensated, uncredited, and unacknowledged." The drama reached a fever pitch on Tuesday when OpenAI announced its agents had solved the Navier-Stokes equations, a 90-year-old set of mathematical formulas that can predict how liquids and gases move. Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematician who, alongside another academic, published research on the problem on Monday, said on Tuesday that OpenAI might have used his conversations with AI chatbots, including OpenAI's, to arrive at a solution. OpenAI said it couldn't rule out that "de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models." The mathematicians also said they believed the CalTech event would serve as unfair advertising for AI companies, who "will take credit for the effort of talented undergrads." Anthropic, which is also sponsoring the event, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. Nor did OpenAI. The "mathathon" is billed as a practice ground for young mathematicians to "responsibly use AI tools to augment human understanding of mathematics," according to an application page. Event organizers, many of whom are undergraduates, said in a response letter on Thursday that they didn't intend to cause such a stir. "Events like Mathathon encourage young people to stay excited about mathematics, engage their interests with modern tools, and maintain hope in a confusing time," the organizers wrote. "It's our first time running an event at this scale, and we are grateful for all the feedback we have received." As designed, participants in the mathathon will compete in a first round, where they're given 40 hours and $20,000 in tokens to solve an open problem. Then, a certain number of teams whose answers are "promising and well explained" will advance to the second round, where they receive six months and additional AI tokens to further their work. Anthropic and OpenAI agreed to support the event by donating $2 million in AI credits. It was unclear on Thursday how many of those tokens were provided by OpenAI, and what happens to them now.

item.title: At 18, I ran home yelling, 'We're rich!' My dad quickly proved me wrong.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.14
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Charles Bonfiglio, CEO of Tint World. It has been edited for length and clarity. I was only 18 when I walked into the family home in Brooklyn and told my mom, dad and sisters, "We're rich!" I showed them the order I'd just received: $1 million worth of products for a young lady's clothing brand I'd designed. I was thrilled, but my dad — who operated a clothing factory in Brooklyn — flipped the paper over and read the fine print. I'd be paid 90 days after delivery, but I'd have to front the costs of production: about $500,000, my father guessed. My dad offered to put his house up as collateral for a loan, but I wasn't the type of kid who was going to risk the family home. So, I called the buyer back and explained I couldn't fulfill the order. I started selling at smaller mom-and-pop shops, rather than department stores, because I could produce clothing as-needed, rather than laying out capital up front. I struggled to get a loan without an established brand I learned an important lesson then: as an entrepreneur, you have to think about a whole business plan, not just creating something you're passionate about. I made decent money with my clothing line, and partnered with my brother-in-law to open a pizzeria. But I dreamed of opening an aftermarket stereo shop. When I'd saved about $30,000 to invest in my business, I moved to Florida to start my stereo shop. I had drafted a business plan that told me it would cost about $80,000. I thought the numbers were great, but the bank wouldn't give me a loan, and a landlord wouldn't give me a lease. Both wanted to work with established brands. My cousin got me into franchising Around then, I attended a family wedding where I talked with a cousin who operated a Meineke Car Care Center. My dad and I visited his shop and saw he was happy, busy, and profitable. On the way home my dad told me, "Charles, take the path of least resistance." I took his advice. In the back of my head I figured I could learn from the franchise, and use that knowledge to open my own business later. The Meineke name opened doors: I was able to get a lease, and a loan through the Small Business Administration. Suddenly, everyone wanted to work with me, because Meineke was such a great brand. Before too long I had three franchises: one to pay the bills, one for my toys — like the brand new Corvette I wanted — and one to pay for my real estate investments. When Meineke started to use computers, I volunteered to test them at my stores. Because of that I had quarterly meetings with all the C-suite executives, where I learned even more about running a business. I bought a company to create my own franchise By 2001 I owned 10 franchises, but I still had the dream of opening the business I'd always wanted: aftermarket auto enhancements. I decided to buy an existing company, called Tint World, where I'd been taking my own vehicles. It had a cool name and six locations, and I would see it working well as a franchise. In 2007, we signed with the first franchisees. I spent the next 17 years building the franchise model I would have wanted during my 30 years as a franchisee. Today, we have over 150 stores, with about 40 more in development. My son convinced me to sell a portion of the business I'd always hoped my son would take over the business, but after his junior year of college he sat my wife and I down and told us we should consider selling. He made some good points: about how hard we'd both worked, and how much we could make even selling a portion of the business. I thought about what my dad had said all those years ago about taking the path of least resistance. In 2025, we sold a portion of the company to a private equity group. Unlike some founders, I loved going through the due diligence process. It gave me a chance to show off the systems I'd built that no one ever saw. Today I'm very, very wealthy. And it all started with the lessons my dad taught me: how to work with my hands and how to work with people.

item.title: The top 15 party schools in the US, ranked
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.00
From which schools offer the best classes to what kind of professional network they want to build, college decisions can be a complicated question for students and their families to navigate. But for some students, it also comes down to one thing: where they'll have the most fun outside class. This year, Florida State University is the place to be. It was ranked the No. 1 party school in the US for 2027 by Niche. Some schools hold large events during homecoming or football seasons, while others keep them going year-round. One school, the University of Miami, for example, has a boat-burning ceremony in which scores of students gather around Lake Osceola in Coral Gables, Florida, to watch a boat burn as part of homecoming events. At some schools, party culture centers on tailgating and football games, while at others, large off-campus parties are the main social events. Every year, Niche publishes a list of the best party schools in the US as part of its annual best colleges list. The site uses student surveys of the party scene on campus, ratings for athletics and Greek life, and access to bars and restaurants based on US Census data to determine the ranking. Whether it's large state schools or smaller colleges with tight-knit communities, these are the 15 schools across the US where students party the hardest in 2026 and 2027. 15. Howard University in Washington, DC Howard University, a historically Black college, was named the 15th-best party school in the US. Known as "The Mecca," the school is the alma mater of key figures such as Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, but that doesn't mean that students sacrifice fun for academics. The Washington, DC, school has a large and engaged Greek life scene. Some students attend "Thirsty Thursdays" parties or darties (day parties) between classes, The Root reported. "The good parties are off campus," one student wrote on Niche. "If you're not a party person, there are so many organizations to be a part of, so you will find your people." 14. Syracuse University in Syracuse, New York Syracuse University was ranked the 14th-best party school in the nation by Niche. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, students marked the end of the school year with Mayfest, a celebration that featured performances and parties. While the tradition hasn't returned, it has inspired different events at the end of the spring semester, such as 2023's "Block Darty." Even as traditions change, Syracuse has kept its party-school reputation thanks to its large Greek life scene. In October, students celebrate homecoming with tailgates, networking events, and open house tours of campus buildings. "The party culture is very fun," one student wrote on Niche, while another added that "the overall culture was overly centered around Greek life and partying." 13. University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa, Alabama With 71 social Greek life chapters, the University of Alabama has been one of the nation's largest fraternity and sorority communities in terms of active membership since 2021. "Bama Rush," a 2023 documentary, took viewers inside the high-stakes world of sororities at the school, showing the fashion, culture, and shortcomings of Greek-life recruitment. "I have loved the first few weeks that I have been part of the UA community," a university freshman wrote on Niche, adding that they'd "made connections with students from all over the country, and that has been an eye-opening experience for me." 12. University of Texas—Austin in Austin At UT Austin, the party scene often centers on game days, campus traditions, and the bars and venues along nearby West Campus and Sixth Street. Football weekends during the fall bring students, alumni, and visitors together for tailgates, concerts, and late-night celebrations across the city. "The party scene is also just as lively as the people here. You'll always be able to find an event on weekends, from frat/sorority house parties to student organization events and an iconic bar street," one freshman wrote on Niche. 11. Morgan State University in Baltimore Morgan State University in Baltimore ranked 11th in Niche's national ranking. Students at the HBCU often gather for large block parties and daytime events, while homecoming brings an even bigger campus-wide celebration. The annual festivities typically include major concerts, alumni events, and parties across campus. "The party life is very lively, there's always something going on, and there is literally something at Morgan for EVERYBODY," one freshman wrote on Niche. 10. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in Champaign, Illinois Famous for its party-school reputation, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ranked 10th among party schools. The school, which is also ranked the best public university in Illinois by Niche, has repeatedly been ranked a top party school. In 2015, the then-university chancellor, Phyllis Wise, told CNN that the school wasn't proud of the label. Still, students enjoy a vibrant party culture, which includes the famous Unofficial Saint Patrick's Day celebration during the first week of March, when students party through the weekend in an alternative to the traditional Saint Patrick's Day, which falls during the school's spring break. One student on Niche described the school as the "definition of study hard, party harder," while another wrote that "the party scene is amazing," and the school is "overall a great place to go to college if you are willing to be outgoing." 9. West Virginia University in Morgantown, West Virginia West Virginia University also made it to the top 10, after Niche named it the ninth-best party school in the US. Located in Morgantown, the school's social life is shaped by Mountaineers athletics, Greek life, and campus traditions. Its Greek community hosts more than 70 social, professional, academic, service, interest-based, and honorary fraternal organizations, per the school. "West Virginia University is a big school with a lot to offer for many different people," one student wrote on Niche. "I would recommend it to someone who is willing to go out of their way to find their community. Due to the size and party nature of the school, it can be easy to feel isolated if you don't fit in with the average WVU student. Otherwise, the nature and campus are beautiful, and the academics are great." Another student on the site highlighted the school's other "types of fun ways to spend the night that don't have to involve alcohol" like the free, late-night UpAllNight event hosted by the school every weekend over the fall and spring semesters, which puts on free events like game shows, bingo, trivia, bowling, billiards, and other activities for students who want to party without the alcohol. 8. University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia The University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia, was ranked the eighth-best party school in the nation. The school's party reputation comes partly from its large Greek life scene, in which over 30% of undergrad students participate, the Red and Black student newspaper reported. The school also has a large football fan base, and every year, students and alums celebrate homecoming with parades, tailgates, and other events. "Although the academics are hard, the party scene and friendships made will be worth it all," one student wrote on Niche. 7. The Ohio State University in Columbus, Ohio The social scene on campus at Ohio State is vibrant, with Buckeyes football, student organizations, and Greek life often filling up students' free time. The school's homecoming celebrations are large and historic, with the tradition dating back to 1912. Celebrations last a week and include alumni reunions and a parade. "It is a great school if you are looking to party, be involved, and get a good education," one student wrote on Niche. 6. The Pennsylvania State University in University Park, Pennsylvania Penn State was ranked the sixth-best party school in the US. Student life at the University Park school is often defined by football, Greek life, and student-led traditions like THON, a student-run charity dance marathon in which 400 student organizations and over 16,000 students participate each year, per the school. "There's always something happening, whether it's a club event, a speaker, a game, or just a random Tuesday that turns into a great night with friends," one student wrote on Niche. 5. University of Southern California in Los Angeles The University of Southern California in Los Angeles was ranked the fifth-best party school in the US. The school, which has an acceptance rate of only 10% and a total cost of attendance of over $100,000, per its website, has one of the largest college football teams in the western US. Each year, students welcome the Trojans back to Los Angeles during a weeklong homecoming celebration. Part of the school's party ranking is thanks to its large Greek life scene, which often hosts parties at fraternity houses, welcoming students and their parents, including Will Ferrell. "The social and party life is unmatched," one student wrote on Niche. 4. University of Dayton in Dayton, Ohio The Catholic school balances religious life with its party scene and has a student experience shaped by Greek life, 240 student organizations, athletics, and on-campus student housing, which some students opt for during all four years of undergrad. One of the largest events at the school is Christmas on Campus, when the campus community gathers to welcome children from the Dayton community to a tree-lighting ceremony, a mass, winter displays, and seasonal foods like hot cocoa and decorated cookies. "You won't feel as if you don't have a friend," one student wrote on Niche. "Partying and the weekend are a big part of campus life," another said. One student mentioned that the weekend often starts as early as Wednesday for students at the school. 3. University of Wisconsin—Madison in Madison, Wisconsin The University of Wisconsin—Madison was ranked third on the list. Students at UW—Madison have access to various social activities, including recreational, leadership-based, and philanthropic activities. The school also has more than 60 Greek organizations. "There is a good campus life and downtown Madison is a great place for socializing and interacting with others," one college junior wrote about the school on Niche. "Most people here want to see you succeed, and it is a very enjoyable experience." 2. Tulane University in New Orleans Tulane University, which The Wall Street Journal ranked the top party school last year, is the second-best party school on Niche's 2027 list and the sixth-best school for Greek life in the US, per Niche's 2027 ranking. Famous for its spirited campus atmosphere, especially during Mardi Gras, this New Orleans university enjoys its party-school reputation because of its location and front-row access to the city's vibrant culture. In addition to off-site bars and eateries, the college has 25 Greek chapters and more than 200 social clubs, such as the Just Dance Club, the Improv Club, and even a crochet club. One college freshman summarized it best: "The school is the definition of work hard, play hard(er)!" 1. Florida State University in Tallahassee, Florida The best party school is Florida State, which also ranked as the best school for Greek life in the US in another Niche ranking. Sports are a huge part of campus life, with many students supporting a variety of athletics, from football to golf. When they're not rooting for their fellow classmates, students at FSU enjoy being part of the more than 700 clubs on campus. "FSU is a place that accommodates many lifestyles and types of people," a college sophomore wrote on Niche, emphasizing that students with wide-ranging interests could enjoy themselves. "You can have an amazing time here without taking a sip of alcohol or ever going to any of the many nightclubs because there's always something happening right on campus."

item.title: Are electric vehicles really bad for the environment?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.86
"The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral. Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Stepping away from the phaseout, he said, would now be backed by "science." Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral." The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix. Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling. It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM. No new insights in TUM report Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known. Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%. Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles. Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe. Batteries have a high environmental cost Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water. Bieker's ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine. "We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture. Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans. Renewable energy making the case for EVs The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas. But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs. "Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonized and expected to be almost fully decarbonized by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will only strengthen the case even more." Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules. "Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of [internal combustion engine] vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed." Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy. "The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia. EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% of respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns. "We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.41
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China. "Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris. European-crewed spaceflight "We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts." Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station." He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface." "And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board." Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport. The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance. 'Passengers or pilots?' Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space. After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?" The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration. "In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said. Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion). "Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically." Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the dark web
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.34
It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are. So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data. But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail." The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users, where a lot of illegal activity takes place. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records. An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals. The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US. The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network. In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments. Data disclosure could have serious consequences The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants. In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf." Is changing passwords enough? And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union. He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords." To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn. Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible." Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk. State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild tabloid: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results." Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.24
On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions. But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions." Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table." She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong." Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel. Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior." In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations. Russia's threats: just a bluff? It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war." Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded. "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said. "Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels." After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through." Armed Russian crews on board Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk. "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation." Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way. "It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel." Inspections would raise costs for Russia While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it." He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy." This article has been translated from German. What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

item.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.95
It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike. The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now. The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death. Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him. Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus. Seeking German cooperation Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg. One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group. Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi. A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats." "It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there. Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation. Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human. "This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained. Patients require intensive care, isolation He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes. Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever. "If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure. Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious. Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo. The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible. Successful tick tactics Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus. Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area. In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been. Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen. Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there. "Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored." This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members. "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind. "It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW. For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible. "India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there." Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil. At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing. "The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa. She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member. For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship. However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend. "In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh. Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first". However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times. "With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole. "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?" Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned. "India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics." What is BRICS for anyway? BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose. The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP. Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order. "Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa. She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues. There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh. What could the BRICS summit achieve? Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security. While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO. "India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely." Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm." He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve. "With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

item.title: Canada, Ukraine pledge 100-year partnership
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.19
Canada and Ukraine on Thursday signed a declaration vowing to keep a 100-year partnership between the two countries. It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits the country for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials. Zelenskyy and Carney said that Canada had pledged to help shore up Ukraine's air defense. "Earlier today, Canada and Ukraine finalized an agreement to deliver critical air defense interceptors (through) the United States Jumpstart mechanism," Carney said. He said that the package would amount to some 350 million Canadian dollars ($260 million, €218 million). The prime minister said that Canada had provided the equivalent of 26 billion Canadian dollars ($19 billion, €16 billion) in support for Ukraine. "We've provided support for the energy systems and beyond. We'll provide more support," he said. Zelenskyy expressed his graitude for what he described as a "very important" air defense package. "I'm so thankful," Zelenskyy said. "This is very important package of air defense and this is crucial." Speaking ahead of his meeting with Zelenskyy, Carney also emphasized Ukrainians' historical role in contributing to European settlement in the prairies of Canada's western provinces. "Ukrainians help build this province, this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes," he said, referring to Alberta, of which Calgary is the largest city. Canada is home to over a million people of Ukrainian descent. Zelenskyy visits Canada after Norway Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary late on Wednesday for "important meetings and agreements" with Canadian officials. His visit comes on the heels of his attendance at King Harald V's funeral in Norway, where his plane had been delayed by a drone incursion. The Ukrainian leader is in the middle of a flurry of trips and meetings to shore up his country's defenses for the cold winter months. "The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter," Zelenskyy said in a social media post before leaving. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation." Carney's statement added Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction." Zelenskyy had also signaled a desire to meet with US President Donald Trump on the matter before the end of September. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Moscow has consistently increased attacks on fuel and heating infrastructure in Ukraine in the autumn and winter. What is happening on the battlefield? Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region overnight, as well as a seaport in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said. He added that other unnamed sited critical to Russia's war industry had also been hit. Alexander Gusev, governor of Russia's Voronezh region, said that one woman in the town of Borisoglebsk had been killed by falling drone debris overnight and that at least 19 drones had been destroyed while flying over the region. The Russian Defense Ministry said a total of 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight. In Ukraine, Russian attacks hit buildings owned by a major food producer in Dnipro, killing at least two according to local officials. Two Azerbaijani crew members were killed in a drone attack on a cargo ship in the Ukrainian region of Odesa, Ukraine's infrastructure ministry said. Azerbaijan's foreign ministry also confirmed the information, adding that two further members of the crew were taken to hospital in Chornomorsk, Ukraine. While Baku did not mention who was responsible for the attack, Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone strike. Edited by: Wesley Rahn, Dmytro Hubenko If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.08
Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, citing what it described as "provocative and hostile acts." The Algerian Defense Ministry said the country would close its airspace to the UAE beginning on Friday. However, commercial flights to and from Algiers will be allowed to continue until the end of 2026. Relations between the two countries have been strained for years over the UAE's expanding influence in northern and western Africa. What did Algeria and the UAE say about the decision? The Algerian Foreign Ministry said that it had made the decision "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the Gulf country. It added that the UAE had "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable." Algiers said it had given the UAE's ambassador 48 hours to comply with the decision to cut ties. The Emirati Foreign Ministry said that it hoped that the decision would be temporary. "The UAE expresses hope that this decision will be temporary, in a manner that preserves the fraternal ties between the two brotherly peoples," the ministry said in a statement. It said that it "affirms the UAE's appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors." Following the announcement, Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, said that diplomatic relations should be based on "rationality, communication and clarity of interests" rather than "riddles and signals that require decoding." He did not explicitly mention Algeria in his post on X. What are the tensions between Algeria and the UAE? Algeria has in the past accused Abu Dhabi of working to destabilize countries in northern Africa and the Sahel such as Libya, Mali, and Sudan. The UAE has been accused of supporting the RSF paramilitary in Sudan's civil war, a charge it denies. It also backs former warlord Khalifa Haftar's Tobruk-based administration in eastern Libya, a rival to the UN-recognized government in Tripoli. In July, Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune harshly criticized the UAE for its influence in other countries, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows." "We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country." Algeria also severed its diplomatic ties with neighboring Morocco in 2021, accusing Rabat of supporting Amazigh separatists in the coastal Kabylia region and amid longstanding tensions over the territory of Western Sahara. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Several killed in coach crash in eastern Switzerland
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.95
Five people were killed and dozens injured in a tourist bush crash near the alpine village of Susch in Switzerland's eastern canton of Graubünden, police said on Friday. Local police said that emergency response teams had been dispatched to the site of the crash, which took place late Thursday afternoon. Dutch media reported that the bus was carrying tourists from the Netherlands. "These are Dutch customers of [Dutch tour operator] OAD. We cannot yet say how many people have been killed or injured," a spokeswoman for Dutch travel association ANVR told the newspaper De Telegraaf. De Telegraaf reported that 48 people were aboard the bus. The number has not been confirmed by police. What do we know about the crash? Police have not yet shared details on what could have caused the crash. "The Graubünden public prosecutor's office is clarifying together with the cantonal police the circumstances that led to the coach accident," a police statement said. The crash occurred on the road between Susch and the nearby village of Zernez, where the bus collided with a guardrail around 4:45 p.m. local time (1445 UTC), according to Swiss broadcaster SRF. Initial reports cited by Germany's DPA news agency indicate the coach hit a guardrail and veered off the road, overturned and came to rest on its side. SRF reported that multiple helicopters were deployed as part of rescue operations. Swiss President Guy Parmelin expressed his condolences in a post on X. "I am deeply shocked and dismayed by today’s tragic accident involving a Dutch coach in Graubünden," he said. "I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those who lost their lives." "The relevant Swiss authorities will ensure that a comprehensive and thorough investigation is carried out to establish all the circumstances surrounding this accident." Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.95
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is spending the money that his troops have earned fighting in Ukraine to fund a long wish list of projects that were previously beyond his financial reach. South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in May that Pyongyang received at least $7.7 billion (€6.6 billion) in financial aid and economic value from Russia in the preceding three years for committing men and materiel to Moscow's war against Ukraine — and potentially as much as $14 billion. That is a significant amount given that the North's GDP for 2024 stood at $26.6 billion. Kim's support for Russia has been lucrative, and a slew of reports are now identifying where that money is being spent. A portion of the funds is being put aside for the Regional Development 20x10 Policy, unveiled in January 2024 and which aims to construct modern industrial facilities in 20 regional cities per year for the next 10 years to improve living standards outside Pyongyang. Benefiting from Russian money More civil programs are being designed, observers say, although most appear to be earmarked for the "elites" who reside in Pyongyang. "Before the alliance with Russia, the general infrastructure was poor due to a mixture of economic mismanagement and sanctions," said Martyn Williams, senior fellow for the Korea program at the Stimson Center in Washington, DC. "With the breakdown in consensus on the United Nations Security Council and renewed trade with China and Russia, things are starting to move along now," he told DW. "There are several large programs to build factories and hospitals across the country, [Kim] has ordered the development of entire new districts of Pyongyang and there's a rural housing project building tens of thousands of rural homes," he said, along with investment in "the modernization of several sectors of the economy." However, he said, structural problems still need to be overcome. "There is investment going into building, but the large new hospital in central Pyongyang was built some time ago and sat unused for a while, until medicines and equipment could be procured," he said. "North Korea is great at building, but keeping it running is the key — so we look to see if that will happen." IAEA warns of new nuclear facility More of the financial windfall is clearly being put into the military. On Wednesday, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had identified a new uranium enrichment facility at the Yongbyon Nuclear Complex with an estimated 28 cascades of centrifuges. The IAEA estimated that the facility would permit the regime to produce 85 kilograms of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year, enough for four nuclear warheads. Satellite images also show that the North is enlarging and upgrading the west coast port of Nampo and Chongjin, on the east coast of the peninsula, to accommodate a new generation of warships. On Monday, Kim attended the commissioning ceremony in Wonsan of the 5,000-ton destroyer Kang Kon, with the North Korean leader claiming the vessel was capable of launching nuclear weapons and would be able to "deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies." The third area of heavy investment has been in major improvements in roads, ports and bridges. This infrastructure stagnated during years of isolation under international sanctions but is now needed to facilitate the deployment of more troops to Russia and the arrival of advanced military technology, energy and consumer goods in return. On Tuesday, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, with customs posts and warehousing facilities under construction on both sides of the waterway. The bridge underlines the rapidly expanding ties since Kim and President Vladimir Putin announced a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024. The route will permit greater truck-borne exchanges, reduce costs and potentially be used for the transit of North Korean men, weapons and ammunition to Russia. It also further reduces the leverage of sanctions on North Korea. "A lot of these projects, such as improving trans-border rail and road connections, building customs facilities and so on, were started before the pandemic and have followed an on-again-off-again pattern ever since," said Marcus Noland, executive vice president at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington. "After difficult times during the pandemic, which was accompanied by border closure, the North Korean economy appears to have grown for the last several years on the back of Ukraine war revenues and cybercrime." Hinterland 'stagnating' Noland said he has the impression that Pyongyang is faring relatively well economically, along with a number of cities on the China border thanks to renewed trade, "but the hinterland continues to stagnate." While the Ukraine conflict and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have been an economic boon to North Korea, analysts say, it's not clear what will happen when the war inevitably comes to an end. "The North Korean regime could be in a difficult spot if peace were to break out in Ukraine," said Noland. "If the war-related revenues were to dry up, the country could experience an economic decline and associated discontent after a period of rising expectations," he stressed. "I am not saying that it would be enough to destabilize the system, but I do think that a transition to peace in Ukraine could present challenges that would have to be navigated by the regime." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.27
Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday. On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet. German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied. What did Dobrindt say about the shield? Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves." The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units. The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks. Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices. The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage. Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by and large, the start of a real war." He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats. "All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti. He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. New tech planned to boost cyber security Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks. The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs. The newspaper said the government also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks. Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025 The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year. These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks. Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub. The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion. Edited by: Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
