item.title: Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.80
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties. There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade. As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven. "Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank. "Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital. Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself. Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million. Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas. That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere. Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia. "The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added. Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain. Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings. Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021. Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since. Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed. Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University. Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028. With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same. Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston. Japan willing to restore normal ties? Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president. Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar. "I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said. Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so. Will the West reengage with Myanmar? As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them. Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending. Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010. "But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said. Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities. On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now. "I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Digital data leeches: trading on our profiles
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.76
Everyone has secrets. Things they wouldn't tell just anyone – except, perhaps, their dating app. What sort of partner they're looking for. Where they go to look for them. Their sexual preferences, maybe, or details about their health. This information is meant to help the app find suitable matches. Selling the details on to other companies is not in the users' interest. But this is what allegedly happened with Grindr, a dating app explicitly aimed at the LGBTQ+ community. Around 12,000 app users in Britain sued the company, which they said had shared highly sensitive personal information with advertisers — even, in some cases, a user's HIV status. The lawsuit, filed in 2024, was settled earlier this week. Grindr has agreed to pay the claimants a total of 26 million pounds (€30 million; $35 million) – but stresses that this is not an admission of liability. Grindr continues to dispute the allegations, there has been no legal judgement. What happens to the data you entrust to apps? This latest case is just one of many that raise the bigger question of what actually happens to the information we entrust to our apps on a daily basis. For users, an app is primarily just a helpful product. But they are often supported by cloud services, analysis tools, advertising networks and other service providers. They save and transfer data, link and analyse it — often contrary to our interest. Jan Penfrat, a digital policy expert, says that many of the big tech companies want to "make it as difficult as possible for users and regulatory authorities to understand what data is gathered on our devices by which players, and for what purpose." Penfrat works for European Digital Rights (EDRi), a European network of NGOs and experts that campaigns to defend fundamental rights and freedoms in the digital realm. We all know what it's like: An app, a messenger service, for example, is quickly installed, and when it asks if it has permission to use personal data, users will often just click "yes." Phone numbers are stored on servers — without approval But the devil is in the detail. When you install WhatsApp, for example, you give it access to all the contacts in your smartphone. The phone numbers are transferred to the server — including those of people who don't use WhatsApp themselves, and who have not given permission for their contact details to be passed on. "All of this flows into an enormous profile," says Penfrat. Companies like Google then offer so-called "targeting" products based on this data. "This means a car or clothes manufacturer can say: I'd like to address these target groups, and I want my advertising to appear in their Google search, Google Mail, or any of the hundreds of millions of third-party websites with integrated Google advertising," Penfrat explains. Selling data profiles Google is just one of many companies that offer data profiles. Two types of data feed into these profiles. One is the data that every user voluntarily discloses when they state something in their profile, or upload private photos. But in addition, many big tech companies have for years now made assumptions based on the data they receive. "If they have access to my location data and know where I usually am at night, they can assume that this is my home address," Penfrat says. "If, for example, it's in a very expensive part of town, they can immediately make assumptions about my income. If they see: Oh, he has geolocation switched on and he regularly goes to a gay club, then he's probably a member of the LGBTQ community. And all this goes straight into the profile." Strict regulation in Europe The EU already has one of the strictest data protection regulations in the world. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) aims to protect people's personal data and privacy. Other EU digital laws such as the Digital Markets Act or the Digital Services Act are intended to prevent big tech companies misusing their power over businesses and users. US businesses also have to abide by these laws if they offer their services to people in Europe, or observe their behavior. The EU Commission has imposed numerous fines as punishment for violations of these regulations. In 2025, it fined Apple €500 million euros ($580 million). Meta, the company that operates Facebook, was fined another €200 million ($232 million). Google had to pay €890 million ($1.03 billion) in fines this year. That sounds like a lot — but a look at the net profit of the Google corporation Alphabet puts it into perspective. In 2025, Alphabet's net profit was around €117 billion ($136 billion). "So these are sums that a company like Google or Amazon will make in just a few days," says Penfrat. "They just include it in their budget." Dependency on US digital services As a result, it is not that easy for the EU to implement truly effective controls. The tech giants have global infrastructures, huge financial resources, and complex business models. European agencies first have to get past these. Added to this is Europe's dependency on cloud services, operating systems, platforms and increasingly also AI infrastructure that, at least to date, have been provided in large part by US companies. Penfrat criticizes Brussels for lacking the political will needed to take firmer action against these companies, and to better equip European data protection authorities. This article has been translated from German.

item.title: Yemen: Houthis take control of strategic Red Sea port city
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.66
Yemen's Houthi militia have captured strategic points on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes. In addition to the Iran-backed group's takeover of the port city of Mokha yesterday, Yemeni government sources told several news agencies on Friday that the Houthis have now also captured the island of Perim, also called Mayyun in Arabic. Reuters reported that Yemeni government forces said they had withdrawn from Perim, and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, located south of Mokha and closer to the narrowest part of the strait. Mokha is located 80 kilometers up the Red Sea coast from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, while Perim Island is located in the strait itself. Vital Red Sea transport route vulnerable? The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran, sending global oil prices skyrocketing. Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets. The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz. "The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying. Dhubab lies just south of Mokha. Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels intensifying efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline. The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022. The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west. The internationally recognized government has its headquarters in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia. Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine. Edited by: Wesley Rahn, Dmytro Hubenko If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.61
At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday. State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)." The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported. Cause remains unclear Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added. Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards". It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire. The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders. Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.47
When Werner Herzog needed a title for his memoirs, he reached back to one of his own films: "Every Man for Himself and God Against All," the original German title of his 1974 feature known in English as "The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser." For Herzog, perhaps the last wild man of European cinema, it's less a title than a worldview. Over more than 60 years as a provocative, boundary-breaking filmmaker, Herzog has made films on the slopes of active volcanoes, and in the middle of the Sahara. He's filmed in the jungle and north of the Arctic Circle, telling stories of characters who live at the edges of human achievement. Often, in making these films, Herzog has pushed himself, and his collaborators, to the edge as well. Now 84, Werner Herzog shows no signs of slowing down. He's back with a new feature film, "Bucking Fastard," his first drama in seven years, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival. 'Bucking Fastard:' two sisters, totally in sync The film is the story of Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two sisters who speak, think and move in unison. They even share the same dreams and love the same undeserving man. Hollywood stars and real-life siblings Kate and Rooney Mara play the sisters, their performances synced up to an uncanny degree. The film is loosely inspired by real-life twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, who became a tabloid sensation in England in the 1980s. The film's title is a reference to an inadvertent simultaneous spoonerism the sisters made in court, when describing their former lover. In Herzog's version, the Holbrooke sisters, after being rejected by their true love (played by Orlando Bloom), decamp to the wilds of Ireland and begin digging a tunnel in a cave, convinced they can dig their way to the Orkney Islands — a mythical place where true love is possible. Reaching out for the extraordinary The Holbrooke sisters are two ecstatic dreamers striving to do the impossible. Typical Herzog protagonists. Herzog himself sees the through-line. "With 'Fitzcarraldo,' there is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain," he told DW in Venice. Herzog was referring to his 1982 epic adventure drama in which he had his crew actually haul a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle to tell the story of a man who dreams of building an opera house in the middle of the rainforest. Similarly, added the director, "Bucking Fastard" is "the dream of an ideal country, which doesn't really exist." In the world of Werner Herzog, art imitates life, and vice versa. While filming "Aguirre, the Wrath of God" (1972), the story of a mad conquistador in search of El Dorado, Herzog and his crew, including star Klaus Kinski, nearly went mad themselves. In his 1999 documentary on Kinski, "My Best Fiend," Herzog recounts how the actor threatened to leave the film. If he did, the director told him, he would follow him and shoot him dead. Real people, real extremes Herzog is, if anything, even better known as a documentarian and his real-life protagonists are as extreme as his fictional characters. In "Grizzly Man" (2005), he ponders the life of Timothy Treadwell, an animal rights activist who spent years getting up close and personal with bears in the wild, until one of them ate him. "Little Dieter Needs to Fly" (1997) follows the German-born American Vietnam War pilot Dieter Dengler, who survived a harrowing escape from a Laotian prison camp. For "La Soufriere" (1977), Herzog filmed in an abandoned town in Guadeloupe, next to a volcano on the brink of eruption, to talk to the one man who refuses to evacuate. Films as our 'collective dreams' Herzog sees little difference between his fiction and non-fiction films. He admits to inventing scenes for his documentaries, and to filming real events for his features. For "Rescue Dawn" (2006), a feature adaptation of the Dieter Dengler story, Herzog got star Christian Bale to devour live maggots on camera (the director showed him how, gobbling up some himself) and wrestle with a real live snake for a scene. "Film does not have so much to do with reality as it does with our collective dreams," Herzog said. He thinks of himself less as a director than "as a poet." 'Just go out and do it' In his often haunting tales of man's struggle with nature, Herzog aims to achieve an "ecstatic truth" beyond mere reality. His goal, he said, is not to depict the extreme as bizarre or extraordinary. It is to inspire everyone to be extraordinary. "Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range," he told DW. "[The message] is very simple: Just go out and do it." Rooney Mara agreed: "Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that's not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that." A divided response in Venice "Bucking Fastard" is an odd, and oddly funny film, especially for a Herzog movie. "Thank you for seeing that," said Herzog, who argued there is humor in all his films, if you look for it. "Sometimes it's a dark humor. Sometimes it's a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn't understand. For Americans, it's easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it." The Venice audience gave "Bucking Fastard" a warm welcome, but critics were more divided. A few embraced Herzog's new piece of ecstatic weirdness. Most dismissed it as confusing, clunky and utterly nonsensical. An "uddled-mup fairytale," wrote one, playing on the film's mixed up title. Why Herzog still matters Herzog critics are legion, but his fans probably don't care. The 84-year-old director is as popular as he's ever been. He launched an Instagram account last year, even though he still doesn't own a smartphone, and it has become a huge hit with Gen Z. "My younger son does it, he knows how, and he tells me 85% of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old," Herzog said. "And because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden [young people] are discovering it." Mara said Herzog remains an inspiration, as "a singular human being [who] really doesn't give a sh**." Speaking to the German director, she noted: "You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that's what we all want to do." Next stop: outer space? For his part, Herzog is not slowing down. He's already put "Bucking Fastard" behind him and is deep in post-production on his new film and has a Taschen photo book in progress. And he still hasn't given up on his impossible dream: making a film in space. "I spoke to NASA, but they didn't take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon [but] he refused to take me on board," he said. "[But] Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board." Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

item.title: Germany’s Goethe-Institut is closing in Russia. Russians tell DW how canceled exams are upending their plans
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.26
Germany's Goethe-Institut will close all Russian branches by September 13 amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany. The Russian foreign ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens. "All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Secretary General of the Goethe-Institut Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany." DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense. 'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates. Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard. "I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said. DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany. "My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said. It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online. Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years. "This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote. "I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW. "It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote. Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025. 'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions' Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany. "We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians." Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions. "Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries. Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected. "The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote. Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia. "German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants. A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so. President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations." According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

item.title: ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.14
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Rising oil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%. "The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin. The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027. Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches. Economic outlook remains uncertain "The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB. For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services. Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.18
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships. Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet. The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually. Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault. SITTING DUCKS Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues. Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war. In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes. Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz. SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force. Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion. These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion. A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective. RIGHTING THE SHIP The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices. But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them. After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion. item.title: The Powder Keg in Outer Space
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.75
The United States, Russia, and China may not yet be in an arms race, but they are gearing up for one. Washington is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, strategic bomber, and ballistic missile submarine. Russia is developing a heavy ICBM and a new warhead while planning upgrades to its submarines and bombers. China has dug more than 300 new missile silos and fielded air-launched ballistic missiles, and it is developing a new generation of submarines and a stealth bomber. All three countries are making decisions about modernizing their nuclear weapons programs that will bear fruit in the decades to come—a notable reversal after decades in which the United States and Russia dismantled thousands of nuclear weapons and China seemed content maintaining a minimal deterrent. Yet it is in the space sector that the competition is intensifying most quickly. In the past decade, U.S. firms have pioneered highly capable small satellites, sent large constellations of them into orbit, and dramatically reduced launch costs. Russia has parked a satellite in an orbit that almost no other satellite uses, in a band of intense radiation more than 1,000 miles up, in what U.S. officials believe is a testing process for a nuclear antisatellite weapon that could one day take out satellite systems en masse. Russian satellites have sidled up to American and European spacecraft, and a Chinese satellite has towed a defunct spacecraft to a new orbit—maneuvers that demonstrate the ability to linger close enough to inspect another country’s satellite or, worse, eavesdrop on it, jam it, grab it, or disable it. Both Russia and China have tested missiles that destroy satellites; a Russian test in 2021 shattered an inactive satellite into more than a thousand pieces. The United States has demonstrated similar capabilities, though with less fanfare, and President Donald Trump has proposed placing thousands of antimissile interceptors in orbit as part of his Golden Dome project. Golden Dome aims to shield the entire United States from all missile threats launched from anywhere, including from Russia and China. This aspiration will shape the brewing arms competition more than anything else. Whether or not the so-called dome ever materializes, the decision to pursue this defensive buildup has likely already compelled Russian and Chinese planners to rethink their countries’ nuclear force structure. Given the long timelines of weapons development, they cannot risk doing otherwise. Both Moscow and Beijing will now plan for larger offensive forces—more missiles, more warheads per missile, more decoys, and more exotic delivery systems designed to fly under or around space-based interceptors—as well as weapons to attack the interceptors and sensors themselves. This will accelerate an arms race as each side fears losing its ability to retaliate, a fundamental requirement of nuclear stability. If the United States is to head off this dangerous cycle now, it needs to relearn a lesson that helped stabilize the U.S.-Soviet competition in the 1960s: arms control works only when countries agree to place limits on their defenses. GAME CHANGER Arms competition is a symptom of great-power enmity, but enmity alone does not induce an arms race. Powerful countries begin amassing arms when they grow concerned about a change in the strategic balance. The change that Russia and China have been responding to recently dates back to 2002, when U.S. President George W. Bush withdrew from the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, paving the way for the United States to deploy a nationwide missile defense that Moscow and Beijing worried might one day be able to neutralize a retaliatory strike. Washington never created the system they feared. Today, the United States has only 44 ground-based interceptors—which have performed poorly in tests—to defend against intercontinental ballistic missiles. Although a few dozen interceptors is more than the zero the United States had in 2002, this number would be overwhelmed by even a small fraction of Russia’s roughly 1,500 deployed strategic warheads. But instead of responding to the system Washington actually built, Russia and China upgraded their offensive arsenals in response to the system they feared Washington might construct. When Russian President Vladimir Putin stood before his country’s legislature in March 2018 and unveiled a menagerie of exotic delivery systems—such as a nuclear-powered cruise missile, a nuclear-armed underwater drone, and a hypersonic boost-glide vehicle, all designed to evade U.S. defenses—he presented them as Russia’s answer to the U.S. withdrawal from the ABM Treaty 16 years earlier. China’s leaders also objected loudly to American missile defense plans, and over the past decade Beijing has sought to guarantee that it can overwhelm any U.S. defense by roughly doubling its nuclear stockpile and fielding an air-launched ballistic missile and a new submarine-launched missile to complete a triad. China has also practiced the launch of key strategic systems into the Pacific—in September 2024 it conducted its first full-range ICBM test in more than 40 years—and developed an orbital bombardment system that could evade U.S. radars and attack the United States. Both Russia and China have built and tested weapons that can threaten the satellites on which U.S. missile defenses depend. Enmity alone does not induce an arms race. There is always a lag between identifying an alarming shift in the strategic balance and developing a response to it. Budgets and bureaucracy can move at a glacial pace, and internal politics often determine the weapons and strategies a country pursues in surprising ways. In the 1970s, for instance, the Soviet Union developed a new generation of seemingly more accurate missiles, the SS-18 and SS-19—large, silo-based ICBMs that could each deliver multiple warheads to targets across the United States. The program was the outcome of a years-long bureaucratic battle in the late 1960s over how to respond to Washington’s development of the multiple-warhead Minuteman III missile. Chinese engineers, meanwhile, began exploring ways to counter U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s proposed missile defense system, the Strategic Defense Initiative, in the 1980s. But plans to improve China’s space-based capabilities languished for years until the 1999 U.S. bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade. The U.S. government said the attack was accidental—the target was a Yugoslav arms procurement agency—but the uproar loosened Chinese funding for various defense programs, including the development of an antisatellite weapon that Beijing finally tested in 2007 by smashing one of its own weather satellites in orbit. It’s too early to understand fully how internal politics are driving Russian and Chinese decisions about arms development today. Yet leaders in both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. They may have overreacted after 2002, given the underwhelming nature of the missile defenses the United States has actually deployed and the efforts of U.S. officials across several administrations to reassure their Russian and Chinese counterparts that the purpose of those defenses was protection against North Korea and Iran, not to neutralize Russian or Chinese nuclear forces. But now, the Trump administration has explicitly embraced the goal of defending against “peer and near-peer adversaries”—a phrase that in Pentagon usage means Russia and China. This has surely made Moscow and Beijing believe that they were right all along. FICTION NO MORE The United States’ Golden Dome project will supercharge this competition. The space-based interceptors at the center of the U.S. proposal would attack Russian and Chinese missiles in their first minutes of flight, before they released their warheads and decoys, threatening to thin out the retaliatory strike that each country relies on to deter a U.S. attack. Russia and China will be seeking new missiles, warheads, and delivery systems that can breach those defenses. Even if there is some doubt about the viability of the Golden Dome, Russian and Chinese officials are obliged to take it seriously. When Reagan introduced the Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, it was widely derided as “Star Wars”—science fiction. At the time, satellites were too large and launching them was too expensive to send an enormous cluster into orbit, as the project proposed. But today, SpaceX’s Starlink network, composed of thousands of relatively small satellites, demonstrates that very large constellations are feasible. Launching swarms of small, light interceptors to defend the United States from incoming nuclear missiles may no longer be so far-fetched. That is not to say the Golden Dome does not face problems. Missile defense systems have always struggled to be what analysts call “cost-effective at the margin.” An attacker can usually build and deploy a missile (or another warhead or a decoy) more cheaply than a defender can build and deploy enough interceptors to stop it. At the moment, the U.S. military plans to use four interceptors to target each warhead in space, and the kill vehicle—the technology that locates and collides with the warhead to destroy it—is particularly expensive. When North Korea paraded six mockup ICBMs in 2012, the United States responded by ordering 14 more interceptors. What those launchers and any missiles cost Pyongyang is unknown, but it was surely a tiny fraction of the roughly $1 billion Washington spent in response. Nor will the cost problem likely be solved with space-based interceptors. In theory, space-based interceptors might be cheaper than ground-based ones because an interceptor already in orbit does not need a large booster and can target a missile early, while it is moving slowly and easy to track. But even though satellite launches are getting cheaper, just a thin defense against the simplest targets will require thousands of satellite-based interceptors that must be continuously refreshed. A few thousand could easily turn into tens of thousands if the interceptors’ boosters do not accelerate quite as quickly, their sensors are not quite as sensitive, and communication with them is not quite as smooth as U.S. military planners anticipate, requiring a greater quantity to make up for shortcomings in quality. Relatively inexpensive efforts by Russia or China to increase their missile stocks or improve the effectiveness of their warheads would make it necessary for the United States to deploy even more interceptors. Starlink satellites may only cost a few hundred thousand to a million dollars, but they do not have an expensive kill vehicle built in. Those that have that capability are enormously expensive. The last space-based interceptor the United States designed—the Near Field Infrared Experiment, developed two decades ago—cost roughly $65 million per unit, adjusted for inflation. THE DANGER MOUNTS It is tempting to take comfort in the slow pace of an arms race. It is entirely possible that by the time these new systems are ready to be deployed, the conditions in which they might actually be used will have passed. Consider AUKUS, the 2021 agreement reached by Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, to jointly produce a nuclear-powered submarine in response to China’s military buildup. When the first boat enters service in the early 2040s, a China led by a 90-year-old Xi Jinping—if he is even still alive—will be vastly different from the China of today. But slow is not the same as stable. The United States, Russia, and China are now all able to harass one another’s satellites in ways that have real consequences. Private companies would find it harder to operate commercial satellites if international cooperation on tracking space objects deteriorates amid this hostile maneuvering, and they would be on the hook for billions of dollars’ worth of assets that are not and will not be insured against acts of war or sabotage. All three countries are also locking themselves into decades-long force postures without knowing exactly what their adversaries’ forces will look like and despite the fact that space capabilities and frontier artificial intelligence models are advancing on much faster timelines. No one can really predict what technologies will be available in the early 2030s, when the U.S. Air Force hopes to deploy the first Sentinel ICBMs, which will replace the 1970s-era Minuteman III in 400 silos as the land-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent. By then, Chinese missiles may be accurate and numerous enough to threaten those silos. AI-enabled reconnaissance could make mobile and concealed forces far easier to find. Or perhaps new space capabilities or AI-enabled cyberattacks will make space-based sensors, on which U.S. early warning depends, vulnerable in ways no one has anticipated. There is a risk that in their efforts to develop capabilities that threaten their adversaries’ space assets, one of the main players could wind up with a temporary incentive to strike first in a crisis—even if it would prefer not to strike at all. If Russia, for instance, places nuclear weapons in orbit, which it appears interested in doing, it might attempt to use those weapons to wipe out satellites to blind the United States at the outset of a conflict. China may similarly develop dangerous methods for destroying large numbers of satellites, including ground-launched “pop-up” boosters that could loft a nuclear warhead into space and detonate it before U.S. defenses could respond. Chinese military scientists have already published models of such a nuclear detonation. The blast would damage any unshielded satellites in line of sight and, as a 1962 U.S. test demonstrated, leave behind a belt of radiation that would continue killing satellites for months. Because this kind of mass attack in wartime would very likely degrade U.S. nuclear command-and-control systems, Washington would have to take seriously the prospect that such a strike in space could be the precursor to a nuclear strike on Earth. The mere possibility of losing its critical space assets in a surprise attack could push the United States to use its forces early or to delegate launch authority in ways that raise the risk of an accident, to avoid the devastating consequences. TIME TO TALK The fear that rapid technological advances could threaten nuclear stability is not new. U.S. and Soviet planners had the same concern in the 1960s, when missiles capable of carrying several warheads (known as multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs), antiballistic missile systems, and antisatellite weapons became available all at once. The solution they chose was arms control. Arms control agreements aimed not only to reduce the number of nuclear weapons in U.S. and Soviet arsenals but also to provide a predictable basis for force planning. The effort met with mixed success. The 1972 SALT agreement limited the number of U.S. and Soviet missile launchers, and later treaties gradually reduced each side’s deployed strategic warheads from more than 10,000 then to 1,550 today. In the 1972 ABM Treaty, Washington and Moscow even managed to rein in some of the defensive deployments that can induce an adversary to develop its offensive capabilities—which is why the nuclear strategist Thomas Schelling, writing in Foreign Affairs four decades ago, identified that agreement as the “high point” of arms control. But negotiations stopped short of limiting MIRVs or antisatellite weapons, and arms control efforts stalled in the early 1980s; after Reagan unveiled his Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, the project became the chief obstacle to reviving them. A renewed arms control effort can slow today’s arms race. The last remaining arms control agreement between Moscow and Washington, New START, lapsed in February, and for the first time since 1972, nothing limits Russia’s and the United States’ expansion of their offensive or defensive nuclear forces. Both countries—and China—are largely making decisions on the basis of fear and suspicion, not the joint pursuit of nuclear stability. Both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. For now, U.S. plans for space make a comprehensive deal difficult to imagine. Moscow is at least conditionally open to one: Putin proposed in September 2025 that both sides informally observe New START’s limits for a year after it expired, and when Washington did not respond, Russia announced that it would hold to those limits only as long as the United States did. Beijing is less enthusiastic, but Chinese officials have been hinting at what they call a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” Writing on social media this year, Trump expressed interest in a “new, improved, and modernized Treaty that can last long into the future”—a treaty that administration officials have suggested might constrain all nuclear weapons, strategic and tactical, and include China as well as Russia. Yet the U.S. president is equally enthusiastic about the Golden Dome. Ultimately, these ambitions are in tension: Trump can have the treaty or the dome, but not both. Neither Moscow nor Beijing will limit their offensive forces or growing space capabilities without at least some predictability regarding the American defenses those forces are intended to defeat. Limiting offenses without also limiting defenses might allow the United States, in a crisis, to attempt a surprise attack on Russia or China and then rely on its powerful defenses to neutralize any surviving forces. This would leave Russia and China unable to retaliate and, as a result, vulnerable to coercion. The good news is that because most countries have a stake in expanding the commercial use of space, they have reason to try to reduce the dangers in that domain alongside efforts to negotiate a new treaty to limit strategic arms. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which the United States, Russia, and China are all parties, already bans placing nuclear weapons in space. It lacks verification, but this problem could be addressed if the signatories agreed to inspections of payloads either before launch or, in extraordinary cases, while in orbit. Every country with satellites in orbit should support a ban on antisatellite weapon tests that result in debris and pursue cooperation on space traffic control to reduce the risk of collisions. All of this becomes more feasible with some defensive limits in place. The idea of restricting defenses against nuclear attack has long been a third rail in American politics, especially among Republicans. But many former Republican orthodoxies have proved negotiable; the party staunchly supported free trade and NATO, and opposed Russia just as strongly, until Trump decided otherwise. An agreement, moreover, does not have to eliminate defenses entirely. The ABM Treaty allowed each party to maintain two missile defense sites, later reduced to one. What a new deal needs to do is to place verifiable limits on defenses that give the other parties a sense of predictability. Without such limits, the United States, Russia, and China are likely to continue expanding their offensive forces, developing ever more exotic delivery systems, and pursuing new ways to attack each other’s satellites. All three will blame their adversaries for making the buildup necessary, but in truth each country will be racing itself, driven by its own fears and internecine politics. It’s hard to imagine how anyone wins such a race—other than by not running at all.
