item.title: A Great Rebalancing Is Coming
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.09
The trade imbalances that have come to characterize the global economy are fundamentally untenable. China, Germany, and a handful of other economies run large, persistent trade surpluses, while the United States absorbs much of these surpluses by running the world’s largest trade deficit. Sooner or later, something must give. For an advanced, capital-rich economy such as that of the United States, an enduring trade deficit will bring with it either rising unemployment or rising debt, neither of which is sustainable. In theory, the major surplus and deficit economies could agree on a coordinated adjustment in which surplus countries would expand domestic demand and deficit countries would gradually reduce their dependence on debt-fueled consumption, allowing the imbalances to shrink without a sharp contraction in global demand. That would be the sensible solution. But because the major players disagree about the causes of the imbalances, they are unlikely to come to such a solution. China attributes them to excessive U.S. consumption and fiscal deficits; the United States blames foreign industrial, trade, and currency policies; and Europe has yet to settle on a coherent diagnosis. As a result, they all have proposed remedies that are at odds with one another. Beijing wants deficit countries to save more and prefers not to change China’s growth model. Washington wants surplus countries to reduce their surpluses by redistributing income to the household sector. European leaders continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and rules-based trade. This makes the chances of a coordinated response slim. And as the economic analyst Martin Wolf wrote in the Financial Times earlier this year, if there is little prospect of preemptive action, “the second-best option is to prepare for a crisis.” Individual economies are now doing just that. History shows that trade imbalances of this scale almost always end painfully—and that the pain of the adjustment is not distributed evenly. High levels of debt combined with low productivity makes a country more likely to bear the burden of a trade adjustment, but economic and political power can also give it the tools to pass the burden off to others. Among the three main economic players today, China is the most vulnerable, the United States has the most capacity to reduce its exposure, and Europe possesses latent power but a dubious ability to use it. None of their maneuvers to protect themselves are likely to reduce the risk or overall cost of a crisis. The question is only who will feel the brunt of the losses when it arrives. HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF Large, persistent trade imbalances have cropped up periodically over the past century, and they are rarely benign. One such episode occurred during the 1920s, when a surge in American productivity was not accompanied by rising wages. Production soared past consumption, and the United States ran enormous trade surpluses. Europe ran the corresponding deficits, as many countries borrowed heavily abroad to rebuild economies devastated by war. Germany in particular borrowed extensively to finance both domestic growth and its reparations payments. American domestic debt also rose rapidly, much of it to fund consumption and asset speculation. As the imbalances persisted and U.S. manufacturing expanded at the expense of European manufacturing, protectionist pressures intensified. France devalued its currency in 1927, the United Kingdom abandoned the gold standard in 1931, and the same year Germany imposed import restrictions and rationed access to foreign currency. Even the United States, whose manufacturers and farmers complained that weak demand was threatening domestic production and employment, passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act in 1930. The adjustment came in the form of a collapse in global trade during the Great Depression of the early and mid-1930s. Nearly every major economy suffered from the contraction, but they did not suffer equally. Those with large deficits, such as the United Kingdom, recovered more quickly and suffered less severe financial distress than the United States, which absorbed a disproportionate share of the costs. American exports fell faster than imports, domestic investment imploded, banks failed, and bankruptcies surged. Trade imbalances on a large scale almost always end painfully. The next major episode of persistent trade imbalances was the rare case in which the imbalances faded away without causing major disruption. During the 1950s and 1960s, the United States again ran very large surpluses while Europe and Japan ran corresponding deficits. Similar to the situation in the 1920s, these deficits financed the reconstruction of postwar economies as resources poured into infrastructure and manufacturing. But unlike in the earlier period, governments maintained strict controls over capital flows and imported capital mostly to fund investments that generated enough future income to service the associated liabilities. Because the investments were so productive, debt rose little relative to GDP. There was also minimal protectionist pressure, largely because Europe and Japan urgently needed imports and the United States actively encouraged reconstruction in both places. As a result of these unusual conditions, trade imbalances disappeared gradually without any countries bearing severe costs. Four more episodes of trade imbalances would follow, all of them ending in pain for the countries involved. One happened in Latin America during the 1970s. The oil shocks of that period, in which the global price of oil soared from roughly $2 per barrel at the beginning of the decade to around $30 per barrel by the end, generated massive petrodollar surpluses in the oil-exporting economies of the Middle East and other members of OPEC. Much of this was deposited in major international banks that, eager to find new customers, loaned the funds to Latin American and other developing economies, eventually leading to overvalued currencies and large trade deficits. By the early 1980s, rising global interest rates made their debt unsustainable. Debt crises resolved the trade imbalances but left the deficit countries with the overwhelming share of the adjustment costs: recession, inflation, austerity, and lost decades of growth. The next case developed during the late 1970s and 1980s. Japanese productivity growth outpaced Japanese wages during this period, and the country began running enormous trade surpluses. The same happened in Germany, allowing the country’s manufacturing sector to become increasingly competitive internationally. The United Kingdom and the United States ran deficits that accommodated both Japan’s and Germany’s surpluses. Japan in particular saw a spectacular surge in domestic debt during the 1980s, as extremely high levels of investment flowed into projects whose returns fell far below expectations. China has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can. Protectionist pressures rose steadily, culminating in the Plaza Accord of 1985, in which the world’s major economies agreed to appreciate the yen and the deutsche mark against the dollar in an effort to reduce trade imbalances. Yet a real resolution of the imbalances did not come until Japan’s economic downturn in the 1990s, which brought collapsing asset prices, persistent deflation, and years of stagnation. It is difficult to compare this to Germany’s experience, however, given that the 1990 unification of East and West Germany fundamentally altered the economy at precisely the same time. The Asian financial crisis of the 1990s in some ways resembled the Latin American trade imbalances of the 1970s. In the early part of the decade, foreign capital poured into a group of East Asian economies. These economies developed large trade deficits, which were balanced by surpluses in Japan, European countries, and, increasingly, China. Although their domestic and external debt rose rapidly, protectionism remained limited. Even so, when investor confidence broke in 1997, the adjustment was swift and brutal. Currency collapses, banking crises, and deep recessions struck the East Asian deficit countries, while the surplus countries bore few costs. Finally, between roughly 2002 and 2008, Germany accumulated large surpluses after implementing labor reforms that pushed wage growth down relative to productivity growth and caused huge increases in saving. It exported more and more to Greece, Portugal, Spain, and several other eurozone economies, which in turn accumulated deficits financed by rapidly rising debt. Because this dynamic emerged within the eurozone, where most members shared a common currency, countries could not impose protectionist measures and exchange-rate adjustment was impossible. When the 2008 global financial crisis triggered the eurozone crisis, the deficit countries experienced sovereign debt crises, unemployment, austerity, and prolonged stagnation that unwound the imbalances. COST ANALYSIS These events demonstrate that trade imbalances become dangerous when they are accompanied by rapidly rising debt and growing financial fragility in either surplus or deficit economies. If a country with a surplus uses its high savings to finance productive investment at home or abroad, the imbalance can persist for many years without causing serious economic disruption. But if instead its excess savings finance unproductive investment at home or drive high household consumption, asset bubbles, or persistent fiscal deficits in the economies of its trading partners, the whole system becomes increasingly shaky. Protectionism is generally not the cause of trade conflicts, but rather a symptom of imbalances that have endured for too long. Its absence does not make the eventual adjustment less painful. Yet when countries adopt protectionist policies, they can influence where the adjustment occurs and who bears the costs. Whether it is surplus or deficit economies that take on those costs may also depend on which side has the greater ability to use trade, financial, or exchange-rate policies to compel the other to adjust. Deficit countries more often bear the costs when they are politically weak and unable to finance themselves independently, defend their currencies, or restrict capital and trade flows without triggering a financial crisis—as Latin American countries were in the early 1980s, much of East Asia was in 1997, and southern Europe was after 2008. Surplus countries are at risk, meanwhile, when deficit countries have sufficiently strong economies and political systems to reduce their own deficits by restricting imports, limiting capital inflows, depreciating their currencies, or otherwise preventing the surplus countries from exporting their excess savings. This is what happened to the United States in the early 1930s and to Japan beginning in the 1990s. Their trade partners reduced their deficits by intervening to reduce imports and increase exports, forcing the U.S. and Japanese surplus-based growth models to unravel as investment collapsed and exports, profits, and asset prices fell. The main takeaway for governments today is twofold. First, the place where debt has risen furthest without a corresponding rise in productive capacity is most at risk when an adjustment to a trade imbalance eventually arrives. Second, the countries involved in imbalanced trade can take action to push adjustment costs onto others, but their success depends largely on economic power and their ability to wield it. THE CRISIS TO COME Today’s global trade imbalances are unusually large, and the coming adjustment is likely to be especially difficult. China looks most vulnerable. Its debt burden is already among the world’s highest; the country has experienced perhaps the fastest increase in debt relative to GDP in history. Much of this debt has funded investment that has generated progressively lower—even negative—economic returns, including excess residential real estate, underutilized infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity that far outstrips demand. This huge and growing debt burden creates enormous pressure on Beijing to take any steps necessary to avoid absorbing the bulk of the adjustment costs. China will almost certainly try to push as much of this burden as possible onto its trade partners. It has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can, allowing excess production to be absorbed abroad rather than forcing a sharp contraction in domestic production and employment. In doing so, China can spread the adjustment over many years as it gradually works down its debt, while its trading partners endure greater costs in the form of larger trade deficits, rising debt, deindustrialization, or weaker growth. If foreign protectionist measures or weaker external demand make this strategy impossible, however, China’s economy would face some combination of slower growth, rising unemployment, falling investment, and financial distress. Whether Beijing can offload the costs of adjustment depends on the willingness of the rest of the world to absorb them. Washington has little reason to continue allowing large, persistent trade deficits. As the world’s largest economy and by far its largest source of demand, the United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit and stop acting as the world’s consumer of last resort. And because U.S. trade policy is centralized within the executive branch—with the president able to impose tariffs, investment restrictions, and export controls under broad statutory authority—Washington has the political ability to exercise this power. If the United States uses industrial policy to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and, more important, takes greater control over its trade and capital flows using tariffs and other restrictive measures, China and other major surplus economies will not be able to maintain their surpluses with corresponding U.S. deficits. They will have to either reduce those surpluses with a painful contraction in domestic production or find new importers among countries that remain both willing and able to absorb them. The United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit. This leaves Europe in perhaps the most difficult position. The eurozone is the world’s third-largest economy and its second-largest source of demand, so Europe has economic power at its disposal. What is much less clear is whether it has the political ability to exercise this power, given its fragmented policymaking institutions and the often divergent interests of its member states. If the United States is able to reduce its trade deficit and expand its share of global manufacturing while China resists an equivalent contraction in its surpluses, a politically divided Europe could be forced to take on larger deficits almost by default. The costs could include deindustrialization, rising debt, and weaker growth. This process may have begun already. Once the major economies stop asking how to minimize the global costs of adjustment and begin asking instead how to minimize their own risk, the opportunity to find a relatively painless solution to the global trade imbalance will have passed. Beijing seems set on trying to preserve its surpluses for as long as possible. Washington is just as intent on reducing its deficits. If Europe can develop the political capacity to do the same, the burden of adjustment will increasingly fall onto the surplus economies, which would have to rely more on domestic demand and less on exports. If it cannot, Europe will absorb more and more of the global surpluses, and what appears today to be a trade conflict mainly between China and the United States may become a conflict between China and Europe—and a struggle between the two of them to avoid bearing steeper costs down the road. History makes clear that trade imbalances are always resolved eventually. What remains uncertain is how damaging the resolution will be—and for whom. item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.90
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement. item.title: Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.76
Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire Failed wars are predictable, if you know what to look for. In a world where great-power competition is intensifying, a revealing test of foreign-policy acumen is a country’s ability to avoid costly conflicts or other endeavors that waste resources, divert attention, and ultimately leave them weaker rather than stronger. In other words: staying out of quagmires. Great powers are often happy to see their rivals stumble into strategic quicksand and may even try to encourage such developments, but wise leaders try to stay out of this kind of trouble. In recent decades, China has done a far better job of avoiding quagmires than either the United States or Russia. Post-Cold War hubris led U.S. leaders to take on a vast array of global responsibilities, some that made sense but many that did not. The “forever wars” in Iraq and Afghanistan are the most obvious examples of the latter, of course, but the United States also gotten itself mired in lesser conflicts in Libya, Yemen, Syria, and various parts of Africa, largely as part of the “global war on terror.” In a world where great-power competition is intensifying, a revealing test of foreign-policy acumen is a country’s ability to avoid costly conflicts or other endeavors that waste resources, divert attention, and ultimately leave them weaker rather than stronger. In other words: staying out of quagmires. Great powers are often happy to see their rivals stumble into strategic quicksand and may even try to encourage such developments, but wise leaders try to stay out of this kind of trouble. In recent decades, China has done a far better job of avoiding quagmires than either the United States or Russia. Post-Cold War hubris led U.S. leaders to take on a vast array of global responsibilities, some that made sense but many that did not. The “forever wars” in Iraq and Afghanistan are the most obvious examples of the latter, of course, but the United States also gotten itself mired in lesser conflicts in Libya, Yemen, Syria, and various parts of Africa, largely as part of the “global war on terror.” One might add the long, inept, and fruitless effort to broker an Israeli-Palestinian peace, which consumed vast amounts of presidential time and attention and ultimately failed, in good part because Washington acted not as a fair-minded mediator but as “Israel’s lawyer.” And now U.S. President Donald Trump has walked open-eyed into a quagmire of his own making with Iran, one with few if any benefits, increasingly obvious costs, and no obvious exit save a humiliating retreat. Similarly, since 2000, Russia has engaged in a series of frozen conflicts with various neighbors, failed to prop up clients such as former Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych or former Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad, and is now mired the running sore of war in Ukraine. Not only have these actions cost the Russian economy and the Russian people a great deal, but they have also poisoned relations with most of Europe and made Russia increasingly dependent on China. Both Washington and Moscow had reasons for acting as they did, but it is hard to argue that these various adventures left either country in a stronger global position. By contrast, China has stayed out of costly quagmires and focused on building power at home, constructing islands in the South China Sea, expanding its diplomatic presence and influence abroad, insulating itself from foreign pressure by building up stockpiles and reserves, and gaining leverage through its control of raw earths and other parts of global supply chains. To be sure, its growing military power and increasingly assertive foreign policy have alarmed its neighbors and encouraged them to balance against Beijing, but its overall position vis-à-vis both Russia and the United States has improved considerably. China’s approach suggests that staying out of trouble abroad is a pretty smart strategy. So why do states blunder into quagmires, and how might they avoid them in the future? Here are some of the warning signs. Ignorance. Nobody starts a war that they think will be long, costly, and maybe end with being defeated. It follows that if they had known in advance what they were getting into, most leaders would have tried something else. And that suggests that quagmires usually arise from ignorance about the country you’re taking on, the difficulties you will encounter against them, or the ways that other actors will respond. The lesson: If you’re about to intervene in a country that you know very little about, look out. Bad advice. Decisions to intervene don’t arise from thin air; somebody has to come up with the idea and then convince the people in charge to embrace it. If you want to avoid a quagmire, therefore, you should be deeply skeptical of the advice you’ll get from self-interested parties who have their own reasons for wanting you to intervene. It was a mistake for the Bush administration to listen to pro-war Iraqi exiles such as Ahmed Chalabi, who wanted to ride to power on the back of the U.S. military. It was equally foolish for Trump to believe Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s sales pitch for a war with Iran, or to have paid attention to similar blandishments from pro-war voices in the United States. This problem is nothing new. In his Discourses on Livy, Niccolò Machiavelli specifically warns leaders against taking the testimony of self-interested parties (in his case, exiles) too seriously: “How vain the faith and promises of men are who are exiles from their own country. … Such is their extreme desire to return to their homes that they naturally believe many things that are not true, and add many others on purpose; so that, with what they really believe and what they say they believe, they will fill you with hopes to that degree that if you attempt to act upon them, you will incur a fruitless expense, or engage in an undertaking that will involve you in ruin.” Notice that the first two problems reinforce each other. The more ignorant one is, the greater the tendency to accept the advice of those who claim to know what is going on. Groupthink. States are also more likely to stumble into quagmires when options aren’t debated in a clear and fair-minded way. Overconfident autocrats surrounded by sycophants and loyalists (think Russian President Vladimir Putin or Trump) are prone to making mistakes of this kind, but so are leaders who refuse to listen to dissenting views and are prone to ignoring information that doesn’t fit their preconceived notions. We all have a tendency to overvalue evidence that supports what we want to do and to discount evidence that we’re wrong, which is why leaders seeking to avoid a quagmire should work overtime to hear alternative views and encourage advisors to stress-test the assumptions underlying the case for war. When leaders don’t do this, the combination of ignorance, bad advice, and a biased decision-making process can lead directly to… Overconfidence. Ignorance and bad advice typically combine to persuade decision-makers that success will be easy to achieve, either because the opponent is militarily inferior, its government is fragile and will quickly collapse, the local population is restive and will welcome the invader, or some combination of the above. Sometimes these things are true, but not often, and managing the aftermath of victory can be even more challenging than the purely military task of defeating an inferior foe. If you want to avoid a quagmire, therefore, make sure you have carefully considered what you are going to do if you win. Even more important, make sure you have a Plan B if your best-case theory of victory turns out to be wrong and you find yourself facing a protracted fight. Unreliable local partners. The U.S. experience in Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq, and now Iran teach a similar lesson: Quagmires are hard to avoid when you don’t have competent and reliable local partners. Washington devoted vast sums trying to nation-build in the first three cases, but its local clients were divided, corrupt, and had their own agendas. Trump seems to have believed that unhappy Iranians (of which there are many) would rise up if the regime’s top leaders were gone, a fantasy that entirely ignored the regime’s well-organized security forces and the lack of a well-organized opposition. Putin made a similar miscalculation in thinking that the Ukrainian government would dissolve as soon as his forces crossed the border (or be easily replaced by pro-Russian quislings once the invading force reached Kyiv), a vain hope that revealed his failure to appreciate the intensity of Ukrainian national feeling. Once it is clear that the optimistic prewar expectations were false and that the war will be long and difficult, a new set of problems comes into play. Even if the smart thing to do is to cut one’s losses and disengage, there are at least two obvious reasons why leaders often find it difficult to extricate themselves from a costly quagmire. Credibility concerns. Governments often believe that they must “stay the course” to preserve a reputation for steadfastness and reliability. Former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger knew the United States couldn’t win in Vietnam, for example, and even conceded that it might have been better if the United States had never entered the war. But he insisted that the commitment of 500,000 U.S. troops had “settled the issue of the importance of” Vietnam because he believed—incorrectly—that withdrawing would undermine U.S. credibility and cause other allies to abandon Washington. He knew the war was lost and that Vietnam was of marginal strategic importance, but his obsession with credibility helped prolong the war for six more years. And as Daniel Ellsberg argued in a famous essay, there is a domestic political analogue here. Leaders are often reluctant to extricate themselves from quagmires because they fear the domestic political consequences of an obvious failure. Even when they know that victory is unlikely, they prefer to kick the can down the road and hand the problem off to their successor. U.S. President Lyndon Johnson passed Vietnam on to Richard Nixon, and Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Trump each bequeathed Afghanistan to the person who replaced them. President Joe Biden had the courage to end a war that he understood the United States was unlikely to win but was widely criticized for the (inevitably) chaotic outcome that accompanied the U.S. withdrawal. This may also be why Trump won’t simply cut his losses and end the war with Iran: He’s still hoping that he can achieve something he might be able to package as a “victory.” Good luck with that. Ironically, this fear of domestic political consequences may be misplaced. Saddam Hussein ended the foolish war that he had started with Iran after eight years of fighting and didn’t fall from power, and he remained in charge in Iraq even after his humiliating defeat in the first Gulf War. President Ronald Reagan withdrew from Lebanon after more than 240 U.S. service members were killed in a terrorist bombing, but he was still widely regarded as a tough-minded, hawkish president. Even Biden suffered little long-term damage from disengaging from Afghanistan in his first year in office—that early decision played hardly any role in the 2024 campaign or in Kamala Harris’s subsequent loss. “Victory is just around the corner.” Powerful states also remain stuck in quagmires because they can afford to keep fighting, and because they have the wherewithal to keep trying new approaches. “There’s a lot of ruin in a nation,” wrote Adam Smith, and that’s especially true for countries with large populations and large economies. Even when the stakes are not that great and victory seems unlikely, a great power can keep a dumb war going for a long time, especially if it can rely on an all-volunteer force, run deficits instead of raising taxes, and keep trying new strategies or new weapons in the hope that one of them will provide the key to victory. Look at all the different things that Russia (and Ukraine) have tried over the past four years, or the various options and strategic innovations that the United States attempted during the various quagmires that it has stumbled into. Thus, Americans were repeatedly told that they had “turned the corner” in Vietnam, a mantra that was resurrected and repeated in Iraq and Afghanistan. In the former, Washington tried coercive bombing, an invasion of Cambodia, mining North Vietnamese harbors, widespread use of defoliants such as Agent Orange, the construction of “strategic hamlets” to protect the local population, “Vietnamization,” etc., all to no avail. The 2007 “surge” in Iraq brought some short-term military benefits but failed to resolve the country’s broader political problems, and the analogous Afghanistan “surge” that the Pentagon foisted on Obama in 2009 was equally unsuccessful. Wealthy states can keep trying different options for a long time, and it is always at least remotely possible that a bit more effort will yield success. Upon such hopes are quagmires prolonged. The bottom line is that quagmires occur because getting out of a war is harder than getting into one. If one wants to avoid quagmires, therefore, a deep-seated reluctance to get involved in foreign wars is one’s best protection. States still need capable military forces and a population that is willing to fight to defend truly vital interests, but pursuing wars of choice fought for flimsy or marginal reasons, on the assumption that they will be easy, is a good way to find yourself in conflicts that you can neither win nor easily end. Thus far, Chinese President Xi Jinping and his associates seem to understand this principle better than Trump and many of his predecessors. As long as that remains the case, advantage Beijing. Stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The New Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world. item.title: What Makes a Good Counterterrorism Strategy?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.83
What Makes a Good Counterterrorism Strategy? Three top experts on the terror threat 25 years after 9/11. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The counterterrorism landscape 25 years after 9/11, Germany’s reluctance to punish Russia more severely, and the United States and Iran continuing to exchange fire. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The counterterrorism landscape 25 years after 9/11, Germany’s reluctance to punish Russia more severely, and the United States and Iran continuing to exchange fire. Avoiding Whiplash Twenty-five years after the 9/11 attacks, global jihadism is no longer viewed as the top terrorism threat to the U.S. homeland, and Washington’s foreign-policy priorities have shifted away from counterterrorism and toward great-power competition. But terrorism remains a challenge for the United States both at home and abroad, particularly as its adversaries increasingly look to exploit rapidly evolving technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI). At the Soufan Center’s Global Summit on Terrorism and Political Violence in New York City on Wednesday, John moderated a fireside chat with three top experts—who served and advised both Republican and Democratic administrations—on what a 21st-century counterterrorism strategy should look like. Much of the discussion focused on how Washington can best confront emerging threats. The 9/11 Commission Report attributed the attacks, in part, to a “failure of imagination” from the U.S. government and intelligence community. Asked whether the United States is currently failing to imagine new terror threats to the homeland, Jen Easterly, who served as the director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency from 2021 to 2025, recalled how the Boston Marathon bombers learned how to make explosives via a digital al Qaeda magazine—and related this to the capabilities that AI offers. For instance, she said, imagine AI generating instructions, precision imagery, or even shopping lists for “crude versions” of cyber, biological, and radiological weapons and putting that at the hands of hostile nations, terrorists, and criminals. This is “the world that we are racing toward at world-class marathon speed,” said Easterly, who is now the CEO of RSAC, a leading cybersecurity conference. There have already been examples of jihadi groups, including Boko Haram, using AI to help with a range of activities, from producing propaganda to planning attacks. Partnerships and learning. AI is far from the only technology that’s exposing counterterrorism vulnerabilities for the United States and its allies. Drones and cyberattacks are also major concerns, particularly in relation to state-sponsored terrorism amid the Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran wars. Maintaining and cultivating strong international partnerships will be crucial to confronting such challenges, the experts said. The United States can better understand the threats that it’s facing by communicating with international partners that have faced similar threats, said Chris Costa, who served as a special assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration. “We have to share those lessons,” Costa said. “Our adversaries are absolutely learning creatures,” he added. “They are learning day in and day out. We have to continue to learn as well.” With the Trump administration’s penchant for antagonizing allies via insulting rhetoric (or provocative maps), tariffs, and other policies, there are fair questions to ask about the potential long-term consequences for U.S. intelligence gathering and counterterrorism. The White House’s counterterrorism strategy has also generated controversy, with its focus on going after “narcoterrorists” and left-wing groups (and no attention granted to threats posed by the far right). Experts have said that the strategy is at odds with reality and driven by ideology. In the discussion at the summit on Wednesday, the experts emphasized the importance of having an intelligence-driven, non-partisan counterterrorism strategy. Though Costa declined to directly criticize the Trump administration, he said that building “trust” with foreign partners requires having a counterterrorism strategy that is “based on facts, based on the intelligence.” When asked whether the United States is being complacent in confronting jihadism as it increasingly focuses on other threats, Joshua Geltzer, who served as a deputy assistant to the president, deputy White House counsel, and legal advisor to the National Security Council under the Biden administration, said the “diffuseness of the terrorism threat … justifies speaking about a range of threats,” but that “jihadism’s still among them.” “Whiplash is a really bad way to do most things, but especially counterterrorism,” Geltzer added. “Unfortunately, the adversary gets a vote. We need our resources to be well allocated.” On the Button What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already. Iran war escalates (again). Iran and the United States continued exchanging tit-for-tat strikes near the Strait of Hormuz this week, with Iran claiming that it had targeted 10 ships and fired missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan, a day after U.S. Central Command said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. The Wall Street Journal also reported that Iran has begun producing ballistic missiles again, citing U.S. and Middle Eastern officials. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, meanwhile, seized a key port in the Red Sea, potentially giving the Iranian regime control of a second shipping chokepoint in the region’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Berlin’s Russia problem. Germany recently accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport. Berlin has taken a number of steps to punish Moscow, which has denied involvement, but some critics feel that its actions are far too tepid and won’t deter future acts of hybrid warfare or what some are calling “state-sponsored terrorism.” John and Sam Skove wrote about these developments, and how domestic political concerns are influencing Germany’s approach to this, in a new piece this week. Snapshot Hot Mic The FBI on Wednesday became the latest U.S. agency to release a cyber strategy, and it did so in an unclassified manner for the first time in the bureau’s history. The 17-page document expands on the Trump administration’s broader cyber doctrine, which advocates more offensive cyberattacks against U.S. adversaries—including in partnership with private companies. The FBI strategy “will direct all 56 field offices on how to pursue counter cyber efforts on behalf of the American people,” Brett Leatherman, the assistant director of the FBI’s cyber division, told reporters on the sidelines of a cybersecurity conference in Washington shortly after announcing the strategy onstage. That includes joint operations with companies such as CrowdStrike and Microsoft, which are frequently targeted by nation-state hackers themselves. Asked by SitRep about fears that this would open up those companies to retaliation, Leatherman said that foreign nations “are using industry right now to hack us in ways that are outside the norms of cyberspace operations.” But, he said, the United States has “to do it in a way that is lawful. We have to do it in a way that protects organizations just like you protect our own personnel.” Leatherman also told SitRep that which companies the FBI works with will depend in part on which systems are being targeted and who is best positioned to address a particular hack. “It’s opportunistic based on what the actors are doing in those environments and what capabilities the industry partners bring to that,” he said. Put on Your Radar Saturday, Sept. 12: The two-day BRICS summit begins in India. U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit Ireland. Sunday, Sept. 13: Sweden holds parliamentary elections. The European Union hosts a two-day Arctic summit. Monday, Sept. 14: The International Atomic Energy Agency general conference begins. Wednesday, Sept. 16: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her State of the European Union address. Thursday, Sept. 17: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the European Parliament. By the Numbers 37—The percentage of Americans who say the United States is unlikely to elect a woman president in their lifetime, according to a new survey from the Pew Research Center. That figure is up from 26 percent in 2023. Quote of the Week “This is actual coercion, bullying, and aggression.” —Philippine National Secretary of Defense Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr., holding up a note that he claimed China passed him onstage at a defense forum in South Korea that criticized a 2016 legal ruling on Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea by an independent tribunal in The Hague. FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Welcome to the New Defense-Dominant World by Stephen M. Walt Whiskey Tango Foxtrot Trump used his speech at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday to pledge $5,000 to every adult American if the Republicans win the November midterm election and retain control of the House and Senate. “It will be called the Trump dividend,” the U.S. president said. As many have pointed out, keeping that promise would cost $1 trillion and, as it stands, would likely be illegal. Correction, Sept. 10, 2026: This newsletter has been updated to correct a quote. item.title: The Bab el-Mandeb Problem
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.72
The Bab el-Mandeb Problem Houthi control of a Red Sea port brings Tehran closer to claiming another critical waterway. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fight for control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, record-high global temperatures, and Ukraine’s request for more foreign aid. The Fall of Mokha Houthi rebels in Yemen seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday in their quest to eventually control the vital Bab el-Mandeb strait. The sweeping ground offensive—which pushed out forces allied with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government—raised concerns that the two sides’ fragile 2022 truce may officially be over and that Yemen has returned to all-out war. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fight for control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, record-high global temperatures, and Ukraine’s request for more foreign aid. The Fall of Mokha Houthi rebels in Yemen seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday in their quest to eventually control the vital Bab el-Mandeb strait. The sweeping ground offensive—which pushed out forces allied with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government—raised concerns that the two sides’ fragile 2022 truce may officially be over and that Yemen has returned to all-out war. Renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni forces erupted in July, after the Saudi-led military coalition tried to prevent a plane bringing Houthis back from Tehran from landing at Sanaa International Airport. Since then, the two sides have exchanged heavy fire, including a Saudi attack on a Houthi-run prison on Monday, which killed at least 23 people, and a Houthi operation across Saudi Arabia that same day, which injured more than 70 people. Fierce battles around Mokha in recent days have particularly drawn the international community’s attention, as many worry that Houthi control of the port brings Iran one step closer to claiming another critical waterway. For months, Iranian forces have effectively stopped most commercial traffic from transiting the Strait of Hormuz, through which around one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas previously passed. That has forced vessels to rely more heavily on Bab el-Mandeb, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. However, if the Houthis—an Iranian-backed proxy group—were to transform Bab el-Mandeb into a second choke point, then Tehran would likely turn the strait into another war front, further strangling the already volatile global energy market. Mokha is less than 50 miles from Bab el-Mandeb. Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate oil prices both exceeded $100 per barrel on Thursday in response to the Houthis’ assault. “This is a potentially major strategic shift,” Maged al-Madhaji, the co-founder of a Yemen-based think tank, the Sanaa Center, told FP’s Keith Johnson. “The fall of Mokha—and, increasingly, the prospect of Houthi control over Bab el-Mandeb—would allow them to turn intermittent pressure on shipping into a sustained threat at much lower operational cost.” What comes next remains unclear. Some experts suggest that the Houthis may try to seize Perim Island, a Yemeni territory that sits at the strait’s narrowest point, making it a crucial hub for controlling the flow of maritime traffic; already, the proxy group has reached the Red Sea islands of Hanish. Taking Perim, though, would grant the Houthis a similar position to Iran’s control of Larak Island, which Tehran uses to monitor global shipping and host military activity. On Wednesday, Pakistan warned Iran to rein in the Houthis’ actions or risk triggering a joint defense arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad. Today’s Most Read - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson What We’re Following Turn up the AC. August marked one of the world’s hottest months in recorded history, according to a new report by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service on Thursday. With an average global surface air temperature of 1.65 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, August 2026 tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest period. Last month also saw the highest daily sea surface temperature over the extra-polar ocean (the band of ocean located between 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north latitude) ever recorded, and it wrapped up Europe’s warmest summer in recent history. Copernicus cited the burning of fossil fuels and a strong El Niño climate pattern for the rise in air and sea temperatures. Human-caused greenhouse gas emissions rose 0.7 percent globally last year to hit a record 54 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, the European Commission said on Monday. The world’s top two emitters—China and the United States—each saw their climate pollution rates increase in 2025. These figures lend support to last week’s damning United Nations report, which warned that humanity has lost its chance to prevent some of the worst consequences of climate change, as the world has failed to achieve the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. Zelensky seeks support. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Thursday to discuss opportunities for greater foreign aid and collaboration. “The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter,” Zelensky wrote on X, referring to Russia’s repeated strategy of targeting civilian energy infrastructure during Ukraine’s coldest months. “We will discuss how to strengthen our resilience, support our people, and ensure that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs to defend itself.” Carney reaffirmed that sentiment on Thursday, adding that Canada “remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine’s defense, recovery, and reconstruction.” He vowed to deepen defense, economic, and energy cooperation, and he unveiled another critical air defense package that adds to the billions of dollars that Ottawa has already given Kyiv since the war began in February 2022. Zelensky’s trip to Canada concludes a week of foreign travel marred by difficulties. In a trip to Oslo on Tuesday for the funeral of Norwegian King Harald V, Zelensky’s connection at Moldova’s Chisinau International Airport was delayed due to a drone threat. It is unclear who launched the drone or how close it came to Zelensky’s plane, but Moldovan President Maia Sandu claimed on Wednesday that “a Russian drone forced us to close our airspace temporarily.” Economic woes. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rate by a quarter point on Thursday, bringing it to 2.5 percent—the highest level in more than a year. This was the bank’s second increase since the Iran war erupted in late February, and it signals growing concerns that the global energy crisis will keep inflation in Europe above its original 2 percent target through 2028. “The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period,” European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, adding that the economic outlook going into next year remains “highly uncertain.” Still, Thursday’s increase was not a shock to economists, who expected a rate hike to coincide with recent skyrocketing global oil prices. Renewed fighting in the Middle East has put central banks under greater pressure, threatened critical global supply chains, and worsened bond market volatility. Next week, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, and the U.S. Federal Reserve will separately meet to determine their own interest rates. Traders are predicting that all three banks will increase their rates. Odds and Ends Two men, two shovels, and one pit of dirt. Nineteen teams of two gathered in the northern Hungarian town of Nyergesujfalu on Saturday for a grave-digging competition. Organized by the Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators, the contest for the quickest-dug and most stylish grave aimed to show off this vital trade skill and counter taboos surrounding death. Diggers Robert Nagy and Laszlo Kiss took first place with a winning time of 1 hour and 21 minutes, receiving a cash prize of roughly $640.
