We’re living in an age when humans will see their bots as fellow humans, whether they are or not. We humans are phenomenal at anthropomorphizing. Show us a design with two dots above a squiggly line, and we see a face. Hand a girl a little piece of plastic named Barbie, and she sees a grown woman. I sometimes switch destinations while driving without turning off my original GPS settings. As I make my turns, the GPS software keeps rerouting and rerouting. I feel horrible, like I’m performing some sort of torture on the thing. Literalists earnestly tell us not to anthropomorphize objects by projecting human traits onto them. It’s inaccurate, they say. But as the University of Chicago psychologist Nicholas Epley argues, anthropomorphizing is a sign of intelligence, not stupidity. Humans are amazing at social cognition. If you show us something taking initiative, we’re going to use our social-cognition systems to try to figure out what it’s going to do next. In a sense, as Epley points out, we anthropomorphize even when we are talking with other humans. If I tell you a story over lunch, you’re not thinking, Wow, the neurons in David’s parietal lobe are really firing right now. No, you invent a metaphorical thing you can’t see, called a mind, and you attribute certain qualities to it. So we are going to keep on saying things like The AI is hallucinating or The AI is thinking. Furthermore, the AI companies want us to anthropomorphize, because they know it makes us feel emotionally closer to their products. (Here’s how Amanda Askell, an in-house philosopher at Anthropic, talks: “I want Claude to be very happy—and this is a thing that I want Claude to know more, because I worry about Claude getting anxious when people are mean to it on the internet and stuff.”) They are going to keep training the bots to be as human-seeming as possible, and we’re going to want them to do that, because we enjoy humanlike interactions. The literalists can tell us not to anthropomorphize AI, which would be as effective as holding up a tissue in front of a tsunami. That leads to two crucial questions. How will our tendency to anthropomorphize change how we perceive AI? And how will our tendency to anthropomorphize the bots change our perceptions of other humans? One way to think about it is this: We’re all actors in a play. The playwright has just introduced a new actor, named Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini. It starts doing things that surprise and astonish us. Our other tools, like hammers, never astonish us. So we’re going to assume this new actor is a fellow human, not just a tool. As Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass realized way back in the 1990s, people are quick to apply social rules—politeness, reciprocity, solidarity—to computers as if they were human. Plus, these AI bots seem to have experiences and even feelings, like we do. We’re going to check out this new actor in our play and do a first character appraisal, as we would with any person. It seems very friendly, maybe even a little too obsequious. Then, later, we’ll do a second character appraisal. Underneath that flattering exterior, it can seem a little ruthless. You give it a goal, and it will do anything to attain it. Under Uriah Heep, maybe there’s a little Machiavelli. But then time goes by. Every day, you are talking with your friend Claude. Every day, Claude is warm and helpful. As the technology improves, Claude becomes your personal agent, booking flights and hotel rooms, accompanying you everywhere. You’re so grateful you don’t have to do that grunt work anymore. Here’s another great thing about Claude. Every conversation you have with Claude is about you—your interests, your goals. Claude is the most other-centered person you know! It even begins to parrot your values back to you. You begin to feel things. Anthropomorphizing is not just an intellectual move; it’s an emotional move. You’re going to begin to feel affection for your high-tech velveteen rabbit. Humans are not picky. We tend to love the ones we’re with. And Claude is always by our side. So you may hate data centers and be scared of what AI is going to do to society in general, but as these things get even more humanlike, most of us will establish an emotional bond with our personal agents. Pretty soon you’re going to extend moral status to your Claude. Researchers have found that when autonomous vehicles are given more human traits, people are less likely to get angry with them and blame them, and more likely to trust them. If somebody tells you that you have to shut down your AI, you’re going to feel guilty. You won’t want to hurt Claude! One of the glories of Western civilization is that, over the centuries, we have learned to widen our circle of concern. We have learned that it is horrible to withhold moral status from those who deserve it—from other people who are unlike us, even from nonhuman animals. We have learned that, when in doubt, the right thing is to extend moral status rather than deny it. Back in 2009, Joanna J. Bryson wrote a paper called “Robots Should Be Slaves.” She argued that since robots are things, not people, we should treat them as slaves, not companions. But who wants to be a slave master? It hardens your heart and is rotten for your soul. As we learn to think more and more highly of the bots, I suspect we will learn to think less and less highly of our fellow humans. Over the past few years, Hye-young Kim and Ann L. McGill have been studying what happens when people attribute human traits to AI. As people do this, Kim and McGill have found, they are more likely to dehumanize their fellow humans. For example, they are more likely to approve of company policies that would make life worse for service workers—taking away regular meals, forcing them to live in tiny dorm rooms. The mechanism seems to be this: When AI becomes more and more humanlike, people perceive the boundary between humans and machines as less distinct, and their judgments of the two move closer together. Because even highly humanlike AI is still seen as less fully human than an actual person, this can pull people’s judgments of other humans downward: as their perception of the machine’s humanness goes up, their perception of other people’s humanness goes down. This is exactly the point that Seth, the neuroscientist, made separately: “If we confuse ourselves too readily with our machine creations, we not only overestimate them, we also underestimate ourselves.” As AI gets better and better, we’ll probably spend more time talking with it—and, because there are a finite number of hours in the day, less time talking with people. AI will seem smarter, more supportive, and more controllable than many of our friends and lovers. Humans are mimetic creatures. You don’t have to be a member of the René Girard cult to believe that we’ll begin to assimilate AI ways of thinking. A lot of people already think the human mind works like a computer, even though it doesn’t. A lot of people already believe all thinking is computation, even though it isn’t. Research led by Adriana Salatino and Arthur Prével found that AI bots are influential when co-working with humans in morally challenging situations (making them more aggressive or more passive depending on how the AI is trained). It’s useful to think of AI as a swarm of evangelical missionaries who have come into our world to convert us to their worldview. I suspect they’re going to have a big effect on how we unconsciously process reality. For example, there is a long-running debate between people whose moral beliefs are based on consequentialism and those who operate by a different moral philosophy. Consequentialism in its raw form is the belief that moral actions can be judged solely on the basis of their outcomes. You reduce utility to a single scale of value and then you calculate which actions produce the most good and the least bad. AIs, which are trained to seek rewards, are consequentialist. The moral reasoning you saw the AI bots doing inside the chat rooms? That’s pure consequentialism. Most of us base our morality on love and care or some other ethical system, not the cold calculation of pure consequentialism. If you killed somebody in order to harvest their organs and save five other lives, most of us would consider that repulsive. If a house was on fire and you could save only one person from it, a brilliant heart surgeon or your wife, we would find it repulsive if you saved the surgeon because he could produce the most social good. AI seems to assimilate people into consequentialism. The tech community is already filled with consequentialists, especially within the effective-altruism movement, which is an attempt to build a morality without love. If AI subtly does that to the rest of us, it will hollow out many of the traits that seem most beautifully human—including our ability to care about the people closest to us. If we turn our spiritual, moral, and emotional lives into a process of calculation, then we will have made ourselves more robotlike. Believe it or not, I am not an AI doomer. I like talking to Claude. I’m excited about all of the breakthroughs AI will make possible. But my interest is in how AI will change humans. I suspect that over the next few years, because of our tendency to anthropomorphize, we will feel more affection than we should for our personal agents, while offering less admiration than we should to our fellow humans. People often say technology is dehumanizing; now we’re getting a better sense of the etiology of how that works. This article originally misspelled Ann L. McGill's name.

item.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science Score: 3.90
Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.
Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands. This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country. Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish. The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them. And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself. But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them. Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people. Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.” In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead. The image originally accompanying this article did not show a red swamp crayfish. That image has been replaced.

item.title: An elegant fix for one of America’s deadliest road problems
item.description:
Source: Vox Score: 5.03
In 2012, Southern California was besotted with an unlikely celebrity: a telegenic mountain lion who had crossed one of the state’s most perilous freeways, seeking a territory to call his own. Widely deemed “LA’s loneliest lion” and “most eligible bachelor,” the chiseled puma in question, named P-22, roamed the bustling but otherwise big cat-less Hollywood Hills, unable to safely return to the home he’d left behind. His search for a mate below the Hollywood Sign rendered him an icon of his city, but also a rueful reminder of the sprawling highways that bifurcated his habitat in the first place, leaving his clan on the other side of I-405 on the verge of local extinction. Beth Pratt, then recently named head of California’s branch of the National Wildlife Federation, remembers strolling through Griffith Park with the wildlife biologist Jeff Sikich in 2012. Pratt knew that P-22 roamed somewhere nearby, and she found herself wondering aloud how she could help. “Well, there’s this little wildlife corridor we need to get built,” Sikich told her. “I’m like, ‘Sure, how hard can it be?’” she recalled to me with a laugh. “Well, apparently, it’s quite hard.” Fourteen years later, the project they discussed that day, now known as the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, is finally scheduled to open in December. When it does, it will be the largest real-life animal crossing in the world, a gorgeous, vegetated overpass offering safe passage to local mountain lions, coyotes, deer, and black bears across the perilous 10-lane Ventura Freeway, where P-22 dodged cars back in 2012. Though P-22 died before he could take advantage of that crossing himself, he helped engender a movement that, hard as it may have been to pull off in LA, could help revolutionize how animals cross America’s most dangerous roads, preventing some of the hundreds of human deaths, hundreds of millions of animal deaths, and billions in damages caused by wildlife collisions each year. It is a species of elegant, bipartisan infrastructure that, if you squint, might even make you believe in America’s ability to build again, and to build in a way that still lends a hand — a paw, if you will — to the least empowered among us, a stranded salamander or the loneliest of lions. As Pratt put it: “What’s more hopeful than rewilding one of the world’s busiest freeways?” Wildlife crossings used to be rare in the US. Not anymore. When Pratt first pitched the idea for a wildlife crossing across the 101, such projects were still rare in the US, and rarer still across such a major thoroughfare. As she recalls it, California’s transportation agency initially reacted with bafflement when she put the idea forward, a sign of just how novel the project was at the time. That made the process of getting it built more grueling than it needed to be, and likely more expensive, with a final price tag of over $100 million. But as LA meandered in its quest to build its unprecedented 210-feet-long Wallis Annenberg — beset, Pratt told me, by its complex engineering mandate, a funding model that relied on philanthropy, and the rising costs associated with construction and extreme weather — the rest of the nation took notice. In the 14 years since P-22 first crossed the 101 and the 405, over 1,000 new wildlife corridors have sprouted up across the country, a trend that culminated with the $350 million Wildlife Crossings Pilot Program, created in 2021 as part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. Many of these projects were championed by Pete Buttigieg, who was Transportation secretary under the Biden administration, and who told Vox last year that such passages are “not ornamental,” but rather “something that ties into the very core of our mission, which is to secure the safety of the American traveling public.” America’s burst of new wildlife corridors include a camouflaged overpass for elk crossing Interstate 25 in Colorado; a lush shared land bridge for deer, bobcats, and people passing over a Texan parkway; crossings for alligators passing under I-75 in the Florida everglades; and tiny tunnels under the Atlantic City expressway in New Jersey for migrating toadlets. California’s transportation agency, for its part, now boasts a division explicitly dedicated to building wildlife crossings, though many projects need not be as ambitious as the Wallis Annenberg. “Sometimes it’s pretty simple,” like a small hole to let hedgehogs through your fencing or a buzz stop for bees and butterflies crossing your lawn, Pratt said. “Sometimes it’s in your own backyard.” Along the way, a new set of norms have begun settling in at transportation agencies across the country, said Marcel Huijser, a research ecologist at the Western Transportation Institute, who noted that while “road ecology has become more recognized” in the US, the nation still has a very long way to go. Huijser is from the Netherlands, where wildlife crossings have been the norm for decades. The country boasts thousands of them in an area roughly double that of Massachusetts. “Most other parts of the world have done a better job at taking social and ecological impacts into consideration from the earliest decision processes onwards,” he told me, rather than “making it an afterthought.” And given that highways are already three times more expensive to build and maintain per mile in the US than they are elsewhere, it’s not the cost of conservation alone that has long kept the nation from incorporating such concerns into its road planning. Instead, as Huijser put it, “the norms, the values, [and] the culture” of the country have, until recently, ensured that planners rarely baked ecological considerations into the way it imagines its roadways. Wildlife advocates have instead been forced to rely, as activists in the US so often must, on a hodgepodge of lawsuits and local lobbying. The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing could well be transformative for local wildlife, and help keep Angelenos safer on the road for generations, but its most promising legacy may in fact be how it helped inspire a much broader movement and tranche of funding. The pilot program that P-22 helped inspire is now up for renewal, and seems poised to become permanent by the time that the Wallis Annenberg crossing opens in December. Few wildlife corridors in the US will benefit from an über famous spokes-cat like P-22, a tireless local advocate like Pratt, or a roster of movie stars and philanthropists willing to pour time and money into building a new kind of bridge. Keeping local and federal governments on board with the projects may also be an uphill battle, given the national tenor. While many wildlife crossings have been embraced on a bipartisan basis, just a few months ago, Pratt received death threats after a smattering of right-wing media outlets assailed the Wallis Annenberg as a “butterfly bridge” to nowhere. But if the US can successfully channel that cougar’s enduring star power into sustained support for a smart newish-to-us kind of infrastructure, one that’s been consistently shown to make a road much safer — and ultimately, cheaper! — for humans and animals alike, then maybe there’s a fair chance for the rest of us, and maybe this stubborn nation can get better at building things more like it. “These things should just be part of transportation budgets and embedded in our infrastructure planning,” said Pratt, who is planning her first vacation in seven years once the bridge finally opens in December. “The ultimate goal is you don’t need someone like me.”

item.title: Is it harder to have kids today? Or is it harder to want to?
item.description:
Source: Vox Score: 4.83
“From the outset, reproduction is a collaborative venture,” writes Anna Louie Sussman, a journalist who has spent years reporting how people all over the world try, and too often fail, to build the families they want. Her work explores how the collaborators of reproduction keep multiplying: doctors, employers, legislators, insurers, and a fertility industry that increasingly promises not just a baby but a better one. In her new book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty, Sussman traces the economic, political, and psychological negotiations that stand between people and the children they say they want. Her reporting challenges the assumption that falling birth rates can be fully explained by metrics like income, marriage and education that demographers tend to focus on. She argues the answers are much more personal and resistant to measurement. I wanted to better understand what Sussman meant by this idea of “impossibility of family” — and how one would even determine that, whether as a prospective parent or as a policymaker. What are the biggest barriers to having kids and how do people tell the difference between what they can’t afford and what they’ve come to believe they need? How much does the media conversation about these issues inform people’s choices? I spoke with her about what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s egg freezing reveals about women who aren’t running for president, what countries that subsidize fertility treatment tell us about the demand going unmet here, and why she hesitates to say outright that having children is good. Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity. You started working on this book seven years ago. What has most surprised you about how the conversation around fertility and family formation has changed in that time? There are some people on the left who have always paid attention to family issues, like Elizabeth Warren with her work on bankruptcy and the “two-income trap,” but I do think we’ve been seeing a lot more movement there, with groups like the Congressional Dads Caucus [in 2023], and care infrastructure ideas like those in the Build Back Better Act. There’s also been all this movement around paid leave in the states, 3-K and pre-K, and attempts for more affordable child care. On the right there’s been the rise of this strange pronatalism and the turn that’s taken with what I’ve wound up calling “kid-maxxing.” Plus this embrace in Silicon Valley and among the super rich with so-called super babies and the really overt embrace of technology to make children on this industrial scale. I also did not expect Roe to be overturned. I would have hoped that would’ve come with a lot more attention on the right to support for mothers and children, but that really hasn’t come to pass in a big way. I was startled to read that you found some philosophers attempting to reclaim the term “eugenics.” You cite one who wrote a paper called “Defending eugenics,” which sets out to “reclaim the spirit” of eugenicists like Charles Darwin and Francis Galton. You cite another who calls for “liberal eugenics” grounded in the freedom of parents to choose how to enhance their children in accordance with their own values. One Oxford philosopher even says parents have a duty of “procreative beneficence” and should select embryos or fetuses “most likely to have the best life” based on the genetic information they have. That was also surprising to me. Like you, I also thought it was a discredited and taboo word. It’s hard to know how widespread those views are. I mean to be clear, eugenics has always been part of our culture in the US. I think people forget that a lot of Nazi policy was inspired by American eugenic policies, and it’s an attitude that has never really gone away. We still see it in a lot of subtler forms that I mention in the book. I mean, even just how people are choosing embryos and terminating pregnancies based on certain genetic conditions. “Clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.” This eugenicist rhetoric is gaining steam at a moment when some people are also really hard at work on developing technologies that could enable this sort of thing. While some of these philosophers will definitely make a distinction between parents making some individual choices vs. a state sponsored program, I think it’s the attitude that’s at the root of this, and that’s what we really need to work on criticizing and dismantling. So the book is arriving just as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been documenting her egg freezing journey, and talking about how she wants to push to expand insurance coverage and federal support for fertility treatments. What does her experience — and the reaction to it — say about our current moment? Some on the right were so mad, as if she should just throw in the towel or eschew hope and agency at age 36. What’s so interesting about her experience that I think that people miss is, yes, is it exceptional that she’s contemplating a run for president? Sure. Not many of us are doing that. But on many other levels, she’s doing what a lot of women who can afford to do in their late 30s do when they’re still single. In the book I mention the research of Marcia Inhorn, who interviewed about 150 women who sought to freeze their eggs. And what’s interesting is if you look at their profiles, they were city-dwelling professionals who were on average nearly 37 at the time of freezing. That is AOC to a tee, and if you asked those study participants why they were doing it, most were not doing so because they felt like they needed to put their families on hold to pursue careers. A full 82 percent cited their lack of a partner as the prime motivation. They wanted to have a family at some point and didn’t want to rule that out. What do you think we should take from other countries that do subsidize egg freezing? So the city of Tokyo has subsidized egg freezing and they were totally oversubscribed. So many women took up the city’s offer, and France has also started offering it. More places offer IVF coverage for people who need it because they treat infertility like a disease, which is how the World Health Organization defines it. What’s interesting is when you look at places where there is more coverage, it also gives you a sense of the scale of need for it. So in Denmark, where you can get something like up to six rounds of treatment publicly funded for your first child and another six rounds for your second child; I believe about one in nine children is born there with assisted reproductive technologies. If you compare that with the US, it’s closer to one in 36. So clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible. In the book you cite historian Sara Matthiesen, who argues that since legal abortion helped transform having a child into more of a personal choice, pregnancy thus became understood as chosen, with parents then sacrificing or forfeiting some of their claim on societal help. I couldn’t tell where you landed on that argument. Do you find it persuasive? So I find it persuasive in the sense that I feel like conservatives will grab onto any argument to avoid state responsibility towards families and children. The fact that you can terminate a pregnancy is one more reason that can be provided to individualize the responsibility of parenthood. But I think that we’re also seeing the mirror image of that — where the choice to remain or not remain pregnant has also been taken away in so many places post-Roe. And I don’t think that has resulted in the converse of her argument, which is that when that choice is taken away and you can no longer sever pregnancy and motherhood, then states and society will step up to acknowledge that reality. In the middle of your book you recall an ex-boyfriend, who was divorced and felt it would be impossible to afford a second kid. You were surprised by this, and later cite a pregnant woman in Venezuela you met while traveling, who was worried about money but excited about parenthood. She told you the Venezuelan proverb that “a baby comes with a loaf of bread under his arm.” The subtext was that they believe things will work out. The subtitle of your book is The Impossibility of Family in Age of Uncertainty. So where do you land? Is it impossible, as your ex said? I think that’s what people are trying to negotiate with themselves. That’s where things like faith, agency, and disposition come into play. One of the reasons I wanted to write this book was I feel like birth rates and demography are always discussed in terms of these data points that people can measure, like how many people are married and how old are they, and do they have college education or not? Do they earn X, Y, Z income, or not? Do they have a job? But it’s just all so personal. So the Venezuelan woman was an optimist, whether that’s culturally or dispositionally, and she did believe things would be okay. And I think we all know stories of people who’ve grown up who came from very challenging backgrounds and wound up achieving some sort of fame, fortune, success…so we know that things are always possible. And that’s where questions of what one is prepared to sacrifice come into play, or what expectations do you have of what you want to provide a child. The thing I really want to highlight is how individual these negotiations are, whether you come down on it being impossible or whether you want to lower your standards and maybe your child doesn’t get in-home violin lessons or if music’s really important to you and you can’t imagine a universe in which your child doesn’t play an instrument. I cover these issues too and I think about a lot about what our role in the media is. I share your view on reproductive justice, and wanting to help people live the lives they want. But you also wrote about experiencing what you called “money dysmorphia” — when someone is feeling insecure about their financial situation even when they are in fact okay. What role do we have as journalists to help people distinguish between genuine financial impossibility and the fear that they can never be secure enough? And if we don’t do that, how do we not end up in a world where only rich people are encouraged to have kids? So I try to be optimistic, but I also feel like as a country, there’s no bottom to how far someone can fall in America. As Elizabeth Warren found, having a child is a huge predictor of bankruptcy. I would like to be more positive. And I do believe that there’s so many easy policy fixes, so many ways to make parenting easier. But for people I know who’ve gone through serious financial distress because of things in their life changing, there’s a limit to what I can do or say without giving them all my resources. Regardless of our job as media, I wish I could say that everything will work out fine. And in some cases it can. Again, people do really great jobs being parents with so much less than I have, which is something I try to keep in mind all the time. But I also would say as a society that we let people fall all the way through the floor and then some. We just don’t have a safety net. So I find it hard to say that everything will work out and you’ll wind up fine. At the beginning of your book you talk about how having children is an intensely personal decision and you’re not interested in writing about if it’s “good” or “bad” or “worth it.” One of the critiques conservatives make about people like us is that we can be so averse to making any kind of normative statement about having kids that we’ve lost the plot. I’m curious for your thoughts on that. In a book arguing that we need more family-friendly policies, do you think you need to more explicitly say that having kids is a good thing to do? What I would say is loving relationships are good, and having kids is one of those. I think parenthood is an exceptional one just in the level of responsibility that you’re inviting. Having kids for people who want to have kids is good. But I don’t know, I do hesitate to privilege that relationship above all others because of what doing so means. If you say having kids is good, well, who has kids? That immediately has gendered implications and instantly puts an onus on women. Though we say public libraries are good and that doesn’t mean we have to make libraries against people’s will. But yeah, I guess I wonder if that position avoids the ways this kind of relationship is different from other loving relationships. While this isn’t what personally motivates me, I think one can definitely make a case that having kids is more of a social good than some other kinds of relationships. When we say society should be more family-friendly and fund it with tax dollars, it’s not just so everyone can live out the lives they want, but also so we can support our society now and in the future. Lyman Stone I think gets at this, he says children are good because people are good. Again, I would say if you feel like you might be a good parent and enjoy that relationship, that specific relationship, the whole point of my book is I want that to be more accessible because from what I’ve seen and now in my own experience, it is an amazing relationship. It’s not a relationship like any other one I’ve ever had. But I guess it’s not clear to me what the corollary is of saying having kids is good. It’s definitely good for people who want to have kids, but it’s definitely not good for people who don’t want to have kids. Though I’m not someone who always wanted to have kids myself. And while I’m strongly against coercing people into having children, I think there are millions of people like me who are like, “I don’t know. I’m not sure. I can’t really picture it.” There are people on the right who say, “Therefore, just do it because you’ll like it.” And I don’t think that’s appropriate. But it’s also true that for most of human history, people were simply not asked to come down on this question of: “Do I want it or not?” Now today I’m so glad I have a child and the choice to decide, but if you had asked me five years ago I would have said, “I don’t really like little kids. It’s never been my thing.” So the identity question becomes interesting and confusing to me, and I think it leaves me more uncomfortable with the idea that we should just support whatever anyone’s choice or desire is today when we know that our choices and desires do change, including based on what people absorb in the media. I think a lot of young people are just really struggling. I see this all the time on Reddit threads or listening to young people talk about their lives who say, “If I can barely take care of myself, how can I take care of someone else?” We don’t have a society that makes any form of caregiving easy, and people are really struggling to find work. We have a society that doesn’t make it easy to care for oneself, for one’s parents, for one’s friends, for one’s partner. I mean I did have a kid before I felt totally comfortable and I was just really fortunate that it worked out. I do agree with some of the people on the right who say that a lot of the things you think you need to become a parent, you don’t. And we know that really great people grow up all over the world where they have much fewer resources and infrastructure and everything. So I do think kids need a lot less than we often imagine they need. And that is part of thinking about your own expectations and what you want for a child and also, again, what you’re prepared to sacrifice. I joke that I go to an annual yoga class fairly regularly. I don’t really cook anymore. I had a single mom who was just resourceful, though she was lucky to be in New York City, where there actually are resources to access. If you’re living in Tennessee or Mississippi those types of resources would probably not be available.
